item.title: Cardinals reportedly finalizing deal to trade Marvin Harrison Jr.
item.description: The Cardinals have reportedly informed Harrison that he'll be inactive for Week 5 while the trade details are being finalized.
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals are finalizing a deal to trade former first-round wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., per NFL insiders Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport.

The acquiring team has not yet been reported.

Breaking: the Arizona Cardinals are finalizing a deal to trade WR Marvin Harrison, sources tell me and @RapSheet.

The team informed Harrison this morning that he will be inactive for Sunday’s game vs Detroit as details of the trade are finalized. pic.twitter.com/x6n0Hsfzzj

— Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 10, 2026

Harrison has reportedly been informed that he’ll be inactive for Sunday afternoon’s matchup with the Detroit Lions while the Cardinals finalize the trade details.

The Cardinals were reportedly asking for a second-round pick and more in return for Harrison in trade talks, per The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero.

Rumors of a potential trade have heated up in recent weeks following a slow start to his 2026 campaign. The former No. 4 overall pick has amassed a 5-85-1 stat line this season and is averaging just 21.3 receiving yards per game with a career-low 38.5% catch rate.

While Harrison has struggled so far in his career, another wide receiver on the team has found his stride. 2023 third-round wideout Michael Wilson had a breakout campaign last season, with 78 catches for 1,006 receiving yards and seven touchdowns, second on the team only behind All-Pro tight end Trey McBride. Wilson was rewarded for that showing with a three-year, $75 million contract extension this offseason.

This breaking news story will be updated.

item.title: Eagles-Jaguars Film Preview: This matchup comes down to Philly’s defensive front
item.description: All-22 analysis look ahead to Sunday morning’s game.
item.content:encoded:
Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work.

The Eagles are coming to London, and I’ll be there! I would quite like them to give me something to enjoy after the past two weeks, but the Jaguars’ offense is going to make that difficult. I really enjoyed watching Liam Coen’s passing game. Let’s get into it.

Pass Game

Coen blends a Shanahan/McVay-style outside-zone foundation with spread formations and an aggressive intermediate passing game. There is plenty of motion, multiple tight-end personnel, and play action from under center, but he is also happy to spread the defense out and let Lawrence attack from the shotgun. Personally, I think Lawrence looks more comfortable in those shotgun sets. His timing and anticipation have been excellent, and Coen gives him a wonderful variety of concepts to attack the middle of the field.

The first thing that stood out was how the Jaguars change which receiver threatens the defense vertically. You cannot just assume the outside receiver is clearing space for an underneath route. On the play below, the slot receiver gets vertical instead, and Parker Washington makes a fantastic catch. Even the running back’s route contributes by creating traffic for the coverage. These are well-designed concepts that force defenders to communicate and distribute routes correctly. The Eagles cannot afford to lose track of a receiver simply because he is coming from an unexpected alignment. Communication will be very important this week.

Parker Washington is really good. He leads the Jaguars with 228 receiving yards and is their most frequent first-read target. Coen uses him to attack downfield, and he has made some difficult catches. Alongside him, Jakobi Meyers has been extremely reliable, catching 13 of his 15 targets, while Brenton Strange gives Lawrence a productive tight end over the middle. Strange has generated 80 yards after the catch already, so the Eagles need to finish tackles when he gets the ball underneath. Brian Thomas remains another downfield option, even though his involvement has been smaller so far, due to some drop issues going back to last year.

Lawrence is seeing the field well and throwing with real confidence. The Jaguars run a lot of posts, deep crossers, dagger concepts, and double posts. Dagger pairs a vertical clear-out with a deeper in-breaking route underneath, and the Jaguars have several ways to create the space for that throw. Lawrence is anticipating those windows rather than waiting for a receiver to stand there waving at him. Some of his red zone throws are outstanding, too. Coen continues to attack aggressively even with less field to work with, and Lawrence has the arm and confidence to make those throws.

This is a major test for the Eagles’ linebackers and safeties. The Jaguars throw to the intermediate area more frequently than any other offense this season, and the Eagles have not defended that area particularly well. Those deep crossers and in-breaking routes ask linebackers to gain depth, recognize what is developing behind them, and still deal with receivers passing through their zones. After the issues against the Rams, I would expect Coen to make the Eagles prove that they can handle it.

Although I prefer the Jaguars’ passing game from the shotgun, they absolutely can hurt you with play action from under center. The example against the Browns below shows the connection between their running game and passing game. The linebackers react to the run action, and Lawrence attacks the space behind them. The Eagles’ linebackers cannot charge downhill simply because the formation and backfield action look like outside zone. Coen has built passing concepts off those same looks, and the Jaguars have been productive with them.

Some of the receivers Coen has schemed open downfield are almost unfair. The switch release below is a great example. The outside receiver moves inside, threatens a corner route, and then bends back to the post. That changes both the receiver’s position and the direction the coverage expects him to go. If the Eagles sit in basic spot-drop Cover 3 or Cover 2 and let those routes develop without matching them properly, they’ll give Lawrence some very easy throws. Vic Fangio needs his secondary to recognize the releases, pass routes off correctly, and communicate well.

There are opportunities for the defense, though. Lawrence’s aggression can work against him. He wants to get the ball out quickly and attack tight windows in the middle of the field, and I think he has been a little fortunate to throw only two interceptions. Some throws look fantastic when they work but give defenders a chance when the timing breaks down. Quick pressure can hurry him into attempting a pass that he should reconsider. The Eagles’ secondary needs to capitalize when those chances arrive.

The offensive line is the biggest reason I think the Eagles can make this uncomfortable. The Jaguars have allowed pressure on only 27.2% of dropbacks, the fourth-lowest rate in the league. But that does not match how consistently convincing the individual blockers look. Lawrence’s average time to throw is just 2.56 seconds, which helps the offense get the ball away before protection problems develop. When pressure does arrive, 25.8% of those pressures have become sacks. He has only two recorded scrambles so far, so escaping and creating with his legs has not been a significant answer.

Anton Harrison had some really poor reps against the Bengals. Myles Murphy absolutely worked him with power, driving him backward and collapsing the pocket. Jonathan Greenard looks like the most obvious Eagles matchup to exploit that weakness if he is available. The interior is also worth attacking, particularly Ezra Cleveland and rookie Emmanuel Pregnon. The Eagles need to win individual rushes and compress the space Lawrence has to step into. If the coverage can make him hold the ball for an extra beat, there should be opportunities up front.

I would also like Fangio to mix in pressure this week. The Jaguars have been outstanding against four-man rushes but considerably less productive against blitzes. That does not mean the Eagles should recklessly send extra defenders and leave the middle of the field exposed. Their own blitz results have been poor. However, showing pressure, changing who comes, and selectively bringing an extra rusher could help disrupt Lawrence’s first read and force the protection to make decisions. I would use simulated pressures alongside actual blitzes to make it harder for him to identify the same comfortable answer every snap.

Run Game

The Jaguars build their running game around outside zone and duo, with inside zone and pulling concepts providing some variety. Outside zone accounts for 36% of their charted runs, and duo/man concepts account for another 24%. Bhayshul Tuten handles most of the work on those plays. He looks much more comfortable running from under center than from the shotgun in the games I watched, which is interesting given his college background. His timing with the blocking looks better, and he has the burst to turn a well-blocked run into a substantial gain.

Every outside-zone run gaining at least 10 yards this year has come from under center. Their outside-zone efficiency from under center is only around break-even, but the shotgun version has been much worse. There are useful tendencies here for the Eagles to recognize.

I particularly liked the looks with a tight end aligned at fullback. The Jaguars do not use them often, but they have been very effective. That extra blocker can change the picture for the linebackers by inserting into a gap or helping create an angle the defense didn’t expect. Coen also has tight ends and receivers who contribute as blockers. Like most modern offenses, they can make a formation heavier than the personnel label initially suggests. Yes, another week of asking defensive backs to take on blocks by tight ends who can block. Wonderful.

The Jaguars have run well to the left, behind Harrison, even though I was unimpressed with his pass protection. The edges need to hold their position against outside zone, while the interior has to prevent duo from generating movement and opening a second lane for Tuten. He has already forced 13 missed tackles, so getting someone into the right gap is only part of the job. The first defender needs to finish.

Chris Rodriguez provides another option, particularly on inside zone, as he is used less on outside zone runs. I expect Fangio to pay close attention to personnel and alignment tendencies rather than treat every run look the same. The Jaguars use two or three tight ends on roughly 41% of snaps, but those packages still contain credible receiving threats. The Eagles have to fit the run without making themselves too easy to manipulate with play action.

Final Thoughts

This is a difficult matchup. Lawrence is playing well, and Coen has designed a passing game that can expose exactly the communication and intermediate-coverage issues the Eagles have shown recently. I would be surprised if the Jaguars did not move the ball. The Eagles’ opportunity is to create negative plays and take advantage of Lawrence’s aggression, rather than expect to shut down every well-designed concept.

For me, this comes down to the defensive front. Fangio can help with disguise and pressure, but the Eagles need their rushers to beat an offensive line that has benefited from Lawrence getting the ball out quickly. If the coverage holds up long enough for those weaknesses to matter, the defense has a chance to produce sacks and turnovers. If Lawrence can settle into his first read and fire intermediate throws all afternoon, this could be a long game. I’ll be watching it in person, so I would really appreciate the pass rush showing up!

Lastly, if you are in London, let me know in the comments! I’ll be around before the game!

item.title: College football Week 6: 2027 NFL Draft prospects for the NY Giants
item.description: Which players should we watch for the NY Giants in Week 6 of the 2026 college football season?
item.content:encoded:
Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 6 of the 2026 college football season!

We have some awesome games on the schedule today, including one that could be the game of the year and a National Championship preview. I said last week that we’re getting into the meat of the schedule and this week could give us some must-watch scouting tape for the draft process. You always love to see “good against good” matchups, and we’ll get plenty of matchups between future NFL players today.

As usual we’re going to concentrate on positions of perceived need for the Giants. In this case, we’ll be spotlighting an offensive and defensive lineman.

So without further ado, let’s get to it!

(14) Missouri vs. Texas A&M

ABC – noon

Player spotlight: Cayden Green (OT, Missouri)

The Giants are pretty well set along the offensive line, at least for the moment. However, Green is an intriguing player in the mold of Sisi Mauigoa who could change the Giants’ plans if he slips to the second day. Green started his career at left guard and played the position for two years before moving out to left tackle. He reportedly measures in at 6-foot-5, 325 pounds and has the movement skills to play tackle as well as the power to play on the interior.

Missouri has a formidable run game, and we know a big, powerful, and athletic lineman who’s a solid pass protector and powerful run blocker will appeal to the Giants. They can’t (easily) move on from Jon Runyan Jr. until after 2027, but the Giants might not want to wait if the value is right.

Oklahoma vs. (1) Texas

ABC – 3:30 p.m.

Player spotlight: Hero Kanu (DT, Texas)

Let’s get this out of the way right now: First Team All Name.

Kanu has an interesting biography as a German-American and a relative latecomer to football. Kanu grew up in the small town of Geltendorf, which is just west of Munich, and was grew up a soccer player. Unfortunately, there aren’t too many 6-foot-5, 309 pound soccer players (even as a goalie), but Kanu eventually discovered American rules football and decided to swap fußball for football. He moved to America for the chance to play for a major college and eventually enrolled at Ohio State. He spent the first three years of his collegiate career at OSU before transferring to Texas in 2025.

Kanu is only credited with 8 tackles for a loss and 3.5 sacks in his college career, but his production has improved since transferring to Texas and becoming a starter. He was a real problem for Tennessee last week and a consistent presence in the Vol’s backfield as a disruptive force.

The Giants will need to continue to build their defensive tackle rotation, and Kanu could be see his profile rise if he continues to stack games like he had against Tennessee.

(6) Alabama vs. (2) Georgia

ABC – 7:30 p.m.

(Note: the game is still scheduled to be played as of this writing. Hurricane Isaias is bearing down on the Gulf Coast and is expected to make landfall as a Category 2 hurricane.)

I’m deviating from this year’s format for this game, because there’s simply far far too much talent on the field in this game to spotlight a single player. This feels like the matchups between these two teams from a couple years ago, when there were NFL players everywhere you looked and often going against each other. It’s entirely possible that this winds up being one of the best games of the year and a preview of the National Championship.

This is one of those games where my best advice is to watch, enjoy, and take note of the players who jump off the screen.

item.title: Vikings Week 5: Holding on to Grudges and First Place
item.description: Grudges aren’t always bad, right?
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the Minnesota Vikings visit the New Orleans Saints in the Caesars Superdome. The NFC South squad’s season has been up and down as they come into the game with a 1-3 record. Their offense has shown decent production so far this season, averaging 367 yards per game and 26.3 points per game, good for 9th and 10th in the NFL, respectively. The reason for this production, however, is due in large part to the abysmal play of the defense, which often results in negative game scripts and base coverage by opposing defenses. On the defensive side of the ball, the Saints rank dead last (or first, depending on how you interpret the metrics) in points allowed per game at 32, with the Lions at a close second with 31.8.

The table is set for a big day

Coming off a contest where they gave up 45 points to the Atlanta Falcons, I foresee this team coming into Sunday one of two ways: deflated after an embarrassing divisional loss on national television, or as a team that is fired up with their backs against the wall, playing to avoid a 1-4 start. No matter how you slice it, this should be a game in which the Vikings’ offense gets a rhythm and is able to build momentum going into the bye week.

The Vikings are in an excellent position to execute a 5-0 start for the 10th time (in the modern NFL era). Out of the nine 5-0 starts in modern franchise history, the Minnesota Vikings have made the playoffs in seven of those nine seasons. Fun fact: history actually favors the 4-1 start for Minnesota, as they have reached the playoffs 100% of the time in seasons where they start with a 4-1 record.

I will never forget

History doesn’t matter to me as much as ABSOLUTELY CRUSHING THE NEW ORLEANS SAINTS. I know it’s been almost two decades, but I still haven’t forgiven this franchise for what it did to our most (or second-most) promising Super Bowl Season of my lifetime. It’s crazy to me to think that there are Vikings fans who have never felt an intense hatred or anger toward the New Orleans Saints. I know holding grudges is bad for you, but I don’t care. I don’t care that this is a completely different team with an all-new coaching staff and players. I will be singing the skol song with an emphasis on “run up the score” as I will always be craving more points against the Saints. I want to use more colorful language in describing our Week 5 opponent, but I will refrain to avoid getting fined.

A rune for your thoughts

Instead, I will ask a rune. I am only pulling one rune from my pouch while asking the question, “What are we going to see this weekend when the Vikings play the Saints?”

The rune, which presented itself face-up and in an upright position, was Hagalaz. What does that mean, you might ask? Well, what we are going to see on Sunday, according to the mythical stone, is “hail, wrath of nature, uncontrolled forces, destruction.” That, my friends, is what is in store for the New Orleans Saints.

It is time for the offense to take a significant step

This will be the game where the offense gets rolling. With Justin Jefferson (as of Friday morning) potentially suiting up, I can see a hailstorm of bombs and dimes raining all over the New Orleans defense. This should be a game in which Kyler Murray can throw for 300 yards and multiple touchdowns. Now, this hasn’t been the style of our favorite football team so far this season.

It could also be a game in which we see the running game be more efficient than it has been so far in 2026. Many of us witnessed the Falcons bully the Saints into giving up 5 rushing touchdowns last week, so look for a big game from Aaron Jones. However, I feel like many teams, when an aspect of their defense gets thrashed in a game, focus intensely on that unit going into the next week, so I think a pass-first approach is the way to go this week.

A new kind of monster

The Saints have been playing with negative game scripts and in high-scoring contests all season. They may have an advantage if the game turns into a shootout. However, they have not met this defense full of savvy veterans and the students of Young Nasty University. The wrath of nature will come from the mind of Brian Flores and his defense. The uncontrolled forces include the likes of Dallas Turner, Jalen Redmond, Blake Cashman, Eric Wilson, Andrew Van Ginkel, Levi-Drake Rodriguez, Caleb Banks, and Big Citrus. Look for this defensive front to wreak havoc and Shough a quarterback named Tyler into oblivion.

There will be nothing left

Destruction will come in the form of the hopes and dreams of New Orleans Saints fans. I respect them for what they have gone through, but they aren’t blameless here. They didn’t tell Greg Williams to put a bounty on Brett Favre, but they sure as hell cheered it on when he was getting crushed on every other play. Ever since that season, the Saints have had terrible luck in the postseason, including, but not limited to, miracles and no-calls. Good. They deserve it, and I wish them the worst of luck going forward.

The frustration of watching this offense fail to score touchdowns in two of four contests so far this season is still in the back of my mind. With our history of kickers in big games, we need to save as many field goals for the postseason as possible. Will Reichard may go down in history as the best kicker in Vikings franchise history, but in order to reach G.O.A.T. status, we will have to see success in the playoffs. He has to emulate Adam Vinatieri’s postseason clutch gene.

To do that, we have to get to the playoffs and put him in situations where he can make those legendary kicks. Field goals against the 0-3 Miami Dolphins are a waste of his talent and skill. Let’s save those for when we really need them against division opponents and in NFC Championship games (or Wild Card games).

I am very much looking forward to Sunday and am hoping we can relax during the bye week as one of the few remaining undefeated teams in the NFL.

Until Next Skol.

item.title: Tyson Bagent to start for the Chicago Bears, unless he doesn’t
item.description: All signs point to the Chicago Bears starting Tyson Bagent again, but Caleb Williams’ questionable game status does make things interesting.
item.content:encoded:
The only thing we should expect from Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson is to expect the unexpected.

Last week against the New York Jets, all signs pointed to Tyson Bagent getting the first start since he was a rookie in 2023. There were even a couple of prominent NFL insiders who broke the news that Bagent took the majority of the first-team reps during the week of practice, so obviously, it would be Bagent.

Only it wasn’t. Well, it sort of wasn’t, because Bagent did start, but Case Keenum also started, and since Keenum took the snap, the official record books show that the 38-year-old Keenum started a second consecutive game at quarterback for the Bears.

Johnson said he opened the game that way because reports leaked about their intention to start Bagent.

“Well, I got all these memos saying that Tyson was starting before I ever made an announcement, so I wanted to get Case out there,” Johnson said in his postgame press conference. “It was like his ceremonial first pitch out there. Handing off the torch.”

That brings us to Sunday’s Bears clash with the Green Bay Packers.

Johnson said earlier in the week that Bagent would start, and he still may, but Caleb Williams returned to practice today for the first time since injuring his hamstring on September 20, and his game status is officially questionable.

Before Williams was limited at today’s practice, Johnson met the media and discussed what Williams has been doing earlier in the week.

“We’ve got him progressively increasing the amount of running that’s going on, and of course the throwing aspect of it is a big part of his position as well,” Johnson said. “Our guys have a good plan in place, and we’re just going step-by-step with that right now. Every couple of days we’re getting this throwing protocol in and making sure there are no setbacks. So far, so good.”

I assume Ben knew Caleb would get some actual practice time in, but I also assume he’s not quite ready. But this is a great step towards him getting in more side work this weekend, and then if he’s cleared to practice in full, he’ll be in line to start the Week 6 game in Atlanta.

The line at FanDuel Sportsbook hasn’t moved (it’s still Packers +1.5), so the oddsmakers don’t think Chicago will get its QB1 back on Sunday in Green Bay, but this latest development may prompt the Packers to address that possibility.

item.title: Three Things I’m Looking at in the New York Jets vs Cleveland Browns Game
item.description: The Jets look to regain momentum against the first place Cleveland Browns on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
I will be at MetLife Stadium this Sunday to see our beloved New York Jets take on the Cleveland Browns! If you will be too, say hello to fellow GGN Contributor BoyGreen25 and me at parking lot J2 for our tailgate. When we looked at the schedule in June, I specifically picked this game for our tailgate because I wanted to make sure we’d be witnessing a win for our annual (and only) in-person experience. I even figured it could be the Jets’ first win of the season.

Now that the game is here, the Jets are 1-3, and the same fanbase that merely eight days ago was ecstatic about the progress shown in a ‘competitive loss’ is now up in arms and ready to fire the same coach they were so confident in during those moral victories. Perspective is really an interesting concept because I think most fans expected 1-3 or 2-2 heading into this game. I heard zero fans, not even the most optimistic ones, predicting 4-0 or 3-1 heading into Week 5.

Is it the contrast of beating the Titans by two scores in Week 1 to then losing to the Tyson Bagent Bears in Week 4? Was that Week 1 performance so shocking that people got their hopes up and couldn’t fathom finishing the NFC North gauntlet 0-3, even though that was the consensus-discussed scenario all summer? Or is it more that the pain of losing to backup quarterbacks is so painful that losing by two scores to Tyson Bagent just drummed up the decades of PTSD associated with our “Same Old Jets”?

For what it’s worth, teams in today’s NFL lose to backup QBs fairly routinely. The same New England Patriots that just beat invincible Josh Allen and the Bills started their season losing to a backup QB. The reigning Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks lost to a backup QB. Losing to a backup QB is far from a death sentence in today’s NFL. Losing four games straight, however, has a much higher mortality rate. Still, I respectfully disagree that this game is a “must-win.”

Of course, should the Jets win? Yes. Would it go a long way toward quieting the fanbase’s uproar? Yes. But they could lose this game and then win the next three (Patriots, Dolphins, Raiders), and the entire fanbase would be completely revitalized and incredibly hopeful for the Week 9 showdown at Arrowhead Stadium against the Chiefs. The season will have a pulse on Monday, October 12, no matter what happens on Sunday.

Let’s assess some of the things worth looking at during the game on Sunday and let’s see their impact on the final outcome of the game:

Capture the Flag

One of my earliest memories of the Glenn Era is all the bragging he did during press conferences. Glenn blasted the previous regime for all the penalties committed and blamed it on the coaching. He said he would coach the team to be better players, more disciplined, and take specific measures (such as hiring referees for training camp) to right these wrongs.

The New York Jets are currently 4th in the NFL in penalties committed per play. They’ve been penalized frequently in all three phases of the game but have apparently earned the most delay-of-game penalties of any team through the first four weeks of any season this century. If you’re curious who leads the league in penalties per play this season, it’s the Cleveland Browns.

Another fun stat: in Week 5, no NFL defense was more penalized than the New York Jets. They were tied with the Cleveland Browns’ defense, which fell victim to Aaron Rodgers’ infamous hard counts on Thursday Night Football. Between the Jets’ delay-of-game penalties and the Browns’ neutral-zone infractions, we’ll see if any chicanery happens on the lines when these teams match up on Sunday.

The goal is simple – don’t commit penalties. Last week specifically, the Jets lost several interceptions to penalties that could’ve been avoided. It would’ve been incredible to end an interception drought with a downpour of them, but the team’s (lack of) discipline wouldn’t let that happen. Needless to say, had those interceptions stuck, the game’s outcome might’ve been very different.

Pressure Cooker

You may look at this article and say, “yeah yeah yeah, any football game can have the same three things to look at,” and list generic goals of every football game. Every football game, you want to take care of the football, move the ball down the field, and pressure the opposing quarterback. This article matters because it’s not that simple: every team is different and has different things going on. Each team’s different qualities get highlighted when they face off against each other.

Deshaun Watson seems much closer to his Houston Texan form than any other version of Watson we’ve seen in orange. Not only is his accuracy back on all three levels, but he’s also elusive and confident on his feet again. He is third in the NFL for rushing yards among QBs and is only behind Josh Allen in rushing attempts. They have designed run plays for him, but he’s most lethal when there’s blanket coverage downfield, and he finds his lane in the pocket.

This is where I’m calling for the Jets, currently 5th worst in the NFL at generating pressures per dropback (18.2%), to finally generate pressure on dropbacks. To be 4th in blitzes per dropback (33.6%) and 28th in pressures per dropback is a level of embarrassment I’m not ready to fully discuss right now.

There’s been a lot of unwarranted criticism hurled at number two overall pick David Bailey, and some debate about whether it’s a talent issue or a usage issue. If I’m weighing in, I’d lean toward usage, since he’s already dropped back into coverage more times this season than he did in his entire senior year at Texas Tech.

Regardless of the true answer to that debate, it’s up to Aaron Glenn to find some way to get into Deshaun’s face this Sunday. If not, he’ll be free to sit back, diagnose, and scramble as he pleases on his way to carving up the Jets defense. Will we see Will McDonald IV be relevant in any way? My call is for Bailey and Ossai to set the edge and force Deshaun into the middle of the field where the Jets have so many strong tacklers. With all the different things you can say about the Jets this year, you can’t say they’re bad at tackling. It’s been one of their strengths all year.

2-Minute Drill

You may have seen my earlier article about Aaron Glenn’s biggest weakness, and I hope it stays front and center for them every day until they get this monkey off their back. With the first interception in 21 games finally caught, I’d imagine they’ll keep coming here and there for a team that has finally addressed the elephant in the room. The next largest elephant in that room is their horrid play at the end of halves.

After the failure at the end of the first half of the Bears game, the Jets’ streak is now up to 15 consecutive scoreless 2-minute drill attempts. I didn’t do a deep dive into every NFL team’s 2-minute drill history, but in that article I explained that I looked at every team’s 2-minute drills this season, and since everyone has scored points at least once this season, we can say with certainty that this streak of 15 is the largest active scoreless streak in the NFL.

Nick Folk’s game-winning field goal against the Falcons in Week 13 was the last time they scored any points within the last two minutes of a half. Overall, Aaron Glenn’s Jets have scored six times in 34(!) attempts. That is a putrid 17.6% rate. What’s even crazier is how often the Jets end up with the ball in their hands in this situation. Some teams had only two or three opportunities through the first four weeks, while the Jets have had six! So it makes it even worse to have so many opportunities and still come up short so often.

If the Jets are going to end this losing streak, they’re going to need to put points up on the board and be able to swing momentum. There is perhaps no bigger momentum swing in the game then scoring those last-second points. Can the Jets do it? I hope so, I’ll be in the stands this week! Let’s go Jets!

item.title: Steelers mailbag: The biggest challenge presented by the Colts in Week 5
item.description: Answering your questions ahead of Steelers vs. Colts.
item.content:encoded:
We are on the eve of Week 5 Sunday in the NFL where the Pittsburgh Steelers will host the Indianapolis Colts in a contest between a pair of 2-2 teams. Ahead of that, a quick mailbag to answer your questions ahead of Week 5. Let’s dive in.

Q: Was it the right move to trade away Pickett, Jones and JPJ? And was it the right move to trade them to the Cowboys? The Steelers could have probably gotten better returns with the Bears or Lions, like they did with the Claypool trade… – Polamolecules_Dude

A: The problem with comparing every trade to the Claypool trade is that the Bears ridiculously overpaid for Claypool – it was a horrible trade. As for the other three, yes, obviously they should have traded Pickett at the time and I was doing cartwheels around my house when they did. Broderick Jones made sense to move because they weren’t going to keep him, so you may as well get something for him. No, they shouldn’t have traded Porter, they should have given him a normal NFL contract where they guarantee money past the first year. But that’s Art Rooney II for you.

Q: Who wins the OL/DL fight on paper? – ChippedHam

A: I’d say both defensive lines are superior to the opposing offensive lines. Colts left tackle Bernhard Raimann had a tough week last week against Washington, allowing three pressures and a sack. Right tackle Jalen Travis has allowed 15 pressures this season, which is the fourth most in the league, meaning T.J. Watt, Nick Herbig, and Alex Highsmith should be able to get to Jones. The Colts don’t have elite edge rushers, but Grover Stewart and DeForest Buckner on the inside will be a handful all day.

Q: How should the Steelers offense look to attack Indy’s defense in the upcoming game? Where are the Colts weakest? – SteelerSince73!

A: Stopping the run. It’s going to be raining all game, meaning the Colts will feed Jonathan Taylor. The Steelers are sixth in stuffed runs and have only allowed three rushing scores this season. If they can limit Taylor and make Daniel Jones beat them, they’ll be in good shape.

item.title: As Bears intend to build a dome, Mike Ditka would not approve
item.description: The passing of larger-than-life NFL legend Mike Ditka has sparked a flood of great stories and clips from Ditka's time in football.
item.content:encoded:
The passing of larger-than-life NFL legend Mike Ditka has sparked a flood of great stories and clips from Ditka's time in football. Many of them stand out. There's one that's particularly relevant to the Bears' ongoing quest to vacate Soldier Field for a venue with a roof.

In December 1987, as the Bears prepared for their annual trip to the Metrodome in Minneapolis, Ditka went off on football not played in the elements.

"I just don’t like indoor domes," Ditka said. "They weren't meant for football. Football is meant to play it outside and on grass. . . . Indoor domes should be useful for roller rinks. That's all they should be for. Roller skating."

That same week, Ditka skated through the Bears' offices in rollerblades.

"They were a gift," Ditka said. "[Vikings G.M.] Mike Lynn sprung for them. That might refute everything I've heard about him from his players."

The Bears won the "Rollerdome" game, 30-24, on a late touchdown pass from Mike Tomczak to Dennis Gentry.

"I did what I did about the dome for certain reasons," Ditka said after the victory. "To get the pressure off the players and get it on me. And I think for that point, it worked."

Ditka then made a point that hopefully will resonate with today's coaches.

"If people don't like the things I do, that's just a point of life," Ditka said. "There's gotta be some levity in life, and there's gotta be a little bit of fun had. And we take this whole thing seriously, like it's life and death. It's not life and death. We're gonna go out and play as hard as we can. We're gonna be great representatives of the city of Chicago, the Chicago Bear organization. That's all we're trying to do is be something that people can be proud of. But, you know, if I'm not gonna have any fun on my way there, partner, I just — they got the wrong guy, because, you know, I said a long time ago, maybe the NFL is a little bit too staid and true in its ways. Maybe it takes somebody to loosen them up a little bit. And our players do that, so why shouldn't the coach be a little wacky?"

Current Bears coach Ben Johnson seems to already be living that message. With the first game after Ditka's passing coming against the Packers at Lambeau Field, maybe Johnson will take it up a notch.

Back to Ditka's point. Football really is meant to be played outside and on grass. Unfortunately, the indoor ship seems to have sailed. The Commanders, Browns, Titans, and Chiefs are currently moving toward swapping the elements for a roller rink. And the Bears inevitably will join them, whether that's in Chicago, Arlington Heights, or Hammond, Indiana.

Whoever the coach of the Vikings is at the time should show up for the first game to be played there on roller skates, as the ultimate homage to Ditka.

item.title: College football’s top Cowboys draft targets in Week 6
item.description: What CFB game are you most looking forward to?
item.content:encoded:
It’s never too early to check out draft prospects from the best college football matchups, where a future prospect lurks that could be on the Cowboys radar. 

Georgia vs Alabama

Georgia and Alabama are both 5-0 and scoring more than 49 points per game. Georgia counters with one of the country’s best defenses, while Alabama has forced 13 turnovers and already returned four interceptions for touchdowns. This game should expose any weakness because neither team can hide a struggling player from the opponent’s depth and athleticism.

Georgia: Ellis Robinson IV, Cornerback

Robinson has developed into one of the leading cornerbacks in the 2027 class. The 6-foot, 180-pound junior recorded four interceptions and seven pass breakups during his breakout 2025 season. Through five games this year, he has added nine tackles, four passes defended and another interception.

His best quality is his ability to remain connected to a receiver in man coverage. Robinson is patient at the line of scrimmage and his long arms allow him to reach through the receiver’s hands and disrupt the catch without arriving too early.

Why The Cowboys Care

The trade for Joey Porter Jr. changed the immediate picture at cornerback, but it did not remove every long-term question. Porter arrived after extension talks with Pittsburgh failed, Shavon Revel Jr. has continued to battle injuries, DaRon Bland is showing the limitations to his game, and Dallas has already needed several replacement combinations in the secondary this season.

Robinson could give Christian Parker a corner capable of playing tight man coverage or working with his eyes on the quarterback. Pairing him with Porter or Bland would allow Dallas to be more aggressive with its pressure packages because the defence would not need to protect both outside cornerbacks on every passing down.

Alabama: Ryan Coleman-Williams, Wide Receiver

Coleman-Williams remains one of the most explosive receivers in college football. The 6-foot, 184-pound junior has caught 20 passes for a team-leading 376 yards and four touchdowns through five games. He is averaging 18.8 yards per reception and has scored in three consecutive games.

His acceleration is the first trait defenders notice. Coleman-Williams can attack the space behind a cornerback, but his speed is just as dangerous on crossing routes and quick throws. Alabama can move him across the formation and allow him to create yards rather than asking him to run deep on every snap.

Why The Cowboys Care

CeeDee Lamb remains the center of the Dallas passing game, and with George Pickens playing on a one-year franchise tag, the team cannot negotiate a new contract until after the season. His future will become a major decision in 2027.

Coleman-Williams would give Dak Prescott another receiver who changes how a defense positions its safeties. He could stretch the field from outside, or turn a short completion into an explosive gain. His presence would prevent opponents from concentrating all their coverage on Lamb and be an exceptional plan of the team decides to not retain Pickens. 

UCLA vs Oregon 

UCLA has built the Big Ten’s most productive rushing attack under its new coaching staff, while Oregon is averaging 47.5 points and more than 500 yards per game. The Ducks will start Dylan Raiola at quarterback because Dante Moore has been ruled out, placing even more responsibility on Oregon’s offensive line.

UCLA: Wayne Knight, Running Back

Knight followed his coaching staff from James Madison to UCLA after producing 2,039 all-purpose yards in 2025. The 5-foot-7, 193-pound senior has immediately handled the step into Power Four football, rushing 49 times for 445 yards and nine touchdowns through four games. His average of 9.1 yards per carry shows how frequently he has turned a normal running lane into an explosive play.

His compact build works in his favour. Knight stays low behind his blockers and changes direction without taking extra steps. He runs with more force than his height suggests and does not regularly fall at first contact.

Why The Cowboys Care

We all know Javonte Williams is the clear starter,  the uncertainty comes behind him. Emari Demercado was waived before the Tampa Bay game, leaving Tyler Goodson as the current backup and keeping the RB2 role unsettled this season and beyond. 

Knight would offer something different from Williams. Dallas could use his speed on outside runs, screens and option routes while allowing Williams to remain the physical center of the rushing attack. Knight’s return experience could also help him earn an active roster place. 

Oregon: Iapani Laloulu, IOL

Laloulu is the experienced anchor of Oregon’s offensive line. The 6-foot-2, 325-pound senior entered the season with 27 consecutive starts, earned first-team All-America honours in 2025 and was a finalist for the Rimington Trophy as one of the country’s best inside offensive linemen. He allowed only one sack during Oregon’s 15-game season last year. 

His power and balance are most impressive in pass protection. Laloulu has the mass to absorb a bull rush without being pushed into the quarterback, but he also keeps his feet active enough to react when a defender moves across his face. His experience shows before the snap when he identifies pressure and helps the rest of the line understand its assignments.

Why The Cowboys Care

Dallas’ offensive line has struggled to provide consistent protection in consecutive games. Tyler Smith’s return helps, but the Cowboys still need better depth and more competition across the line. Cooper Beebe is the starting center, so this would be about strengthening the entire unit rather than replacing anyone. 

Laloulu could compete at guard, serve as the backup center and give Dallas experienced cover at three interior positions. His pass-protection strength would be particularly useful after the line allowed repeated quick pressure against Houston and Tampa Bay. His center/guard versatility could also protect the Cowboys when injuries force changes.

item.title: NFL Week 5 betting advice: Giants-Commanders picks and props
item.description: Giants-Commanders wagers to consider as you fill out your tickets
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 5 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes!

Here’s something you don’t see every day: The Giants are 3-1, their opponent this week (Washington) is 1-3, and they’re underdogs. New York comes in on a two-game winning streak, albeit with a pair of extremely narrow escapes, at home, over very weak competition.

It gets a little harder this week. The Commanders lost to the Colts in London last week, but for much of the game they were led by a third-string, seventh-round rookie QB seeing his first NFL action. They’ll have Jayden Daniels back this week, and that’s obviously a massive boost. However, they could be without their top two wide receivers. Like the Giants, they’ve had a slew of key injuries on the young season. The Giants are 0-3 against the Commanders with Daniels under center.

With Dallas losing to the previously winless Bucs on Thursday night at home, and the badly wounded Eagles traveling to London on Sunday to face the red-hot Jaguars, the Giants are staring down a great chance to go up two full games on the NFC East if they can upset the Commanders. So it’s a big division game for John Harbaugh’s team, which is trying to find solid footing after the losses of Jaxson Dart and Brian Burns.

I’m on a heater – My picks are 3-0 each of the last two weeks, and I’m 8-4 on the season. I’ll try to keep the streak going in Week 5.

Let’s get to this week’s picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel and are as of Saturday, Oct. 10. The forecast for Sunday is rainy, with some wind too, from tropical storm Isaias.

The line for the game is Commanders -3.5, with a game total of 42.5

  1. Game total UNDER 42.5 (-115). This total feels high to me. Stefon Diggs isn’t going to play and Terry McLaurin is a game-time decision. The Commanders have struggled to run the ball. The Giants are going to want to establish the run, but the Commanders are pretty stout in that regard (sixth ranked defense against the run). They’re susceptible to the pass (24th ranked pass defense), but I don’t think the Giants’ coaching staff wants Jameis Winston to drop back 30-plus times again, if they can avoid it. Throw in the bad weather that’s expected and I think scoring will be suppressed.
  2. Jameis Winston most passing yards in game (-120). Daniels is going to be without some key receiving weapons (although the Commanders will have RB Rachaad White back). Winston has all of his weapons, and I think the Giants are going to have to throw a lot to win this game. That’s how you beat the Commanders. Throw in the re-injury risk with Daniels and his bum elbow and I’ll take Winston to have more passing yards than his counterpart.
  3. Jayden Daniels OVER 30.5 rushing yards (-114). Daniels is supposedly playing without any limitations, but I suspect this line is as low as it is because there’s concern that he’ll run less to protect his elbow. I’m not buying it – he knows his legs are a fantastic weapon in his arsenal, and he’s always been aggressive about taking off when the opportunity is there. He averages almost 50 rushing yards per game for his career, and that average includes several games he didn’t finish. Even if the very athletic Arvell Reese is spying him, I expect plenty of running and especially given the Commanders’ depleted receiver corps. This over feels like free money – provided Daniels finishes the game.

Those are the picks for Week 5. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 5 fantasy preview, with start/sit advice and more, right here.

item.title: Dolphins rule out four for Sunday’s game against Bengals
item.description: Who is out for the Dolphins and Bengals game? Could Miami add two defensive players back to the roster?
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins have ruled out four players for their Week 5 game against the Cincinnati Bengals. The team will miss starters and key players on offense, defense, and special teams. Can they overcome the losses? Will two players return from the reserve lists by Sunday?

The injury lists for both teams were released yesterday afternoon.

Players ruled out: Caleb Douglas continues to miss playing time

Rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas caught 7 passes for 113 yards in Miami’s first two games, but has been sidelined with an ankle injury since. The third-round pick was the first of three wide receivers selected by the Dolphins in the 2026 Draft, joined by third-round selection Chris Bell and fifth-round addition Kevin Coleman Jr. Miami is hoping the three receivers can grow together and provide the nucleus for the team moving forward. Douglas, who is dealing with an ankle injury, unfortunately continues to miss playing time as he recovers.

Joining Douglas on Miami’s injury report with an “out” designation are edge rusher Robert Beal Jr., tight end Justin Joly, and cornerback Reese Taylor. Beal, like Douglas, was injured during Week 2 and has not played since. The Dolphins’ pass rush seemed to breakout last week against the Minnesota Vikings, with the team recording four sacks, and returning Beal, who has a lingering hamstring injury, to the group would add to the attack.

Taylor has a quadriceps injury. He has not seen any defensive snaps this year, but he has been on special teams and his absence leaves a hole there.

Joly sustained a concussion this week, but he has already been inactive for much of the season, making one brief special teams appearance in Week 2.

For the Bengals, safety Kyle Dugger has been ruled out with a quadriceps issue.

Questionable status: Bengals wide receivers, Dolphins running back headline group

The story of the week for the Bengals has been the health of their top two wide receivers, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Chase sustained a concussion during Cincinnati’s Week 4 game, while Tee Higgins has injuries to his groin and neck. Both players are questionable for the game, with no clear indication if they will be available. Chase returned to practice on Friday as a full participant after being limited earlier in the week, but he has not officially cleared the league’s concussion protocol that would allow him to play on Sunday.

Higgins, according to Cincy Jungle, is expected to warm up with the team to see if his adductor and neck will allow him to play.

Cincinnati also listed linebacker Swayze Bozeman (groin), safety Bryan Cook (ankle), and wide receiver Colbie Young (knee) as questionable for Sunday.

The Miami side of the injury report includes running back Jaylen Wright, who continues to deal with a foot injury. The Dolphins are still adjusting following the loss of Pro Bowl running back De’Von Achane to a knee injury suffered in Week 3, with Wright and Ollie Gordon II expected to see increased opportunities without Achane on the field. Wright was able to play last week against the Minnesota Vikings, but he only had five carries for seven yards during the game.

Miami also listed linebacker Jackson Woodard (ankle) as questionable.

Will Miami activate players from their reserve lists?

Miami could make some roster moves ahead of Sunday’s game. Defensive tackle Kenneth Grant is on the injured reserve list with a toe injury, but he returned to practice this week and fully participated in Friday’s workout. Cornerback Storm Duck, working his way back from a knee injury sustained last year, is in his second week of practices as he tries to return from the physically unable to perform list. Duck fully participated in the week’s practices. Both players are officially questionable on the injury report.

If Miami plans to activate one or both players for Sunday’s game, it must make the roster moves by 4 p.m. Eastern today.

The Dolphins’ bye week is Week 6, which could factor into the consideration of whether to activate Grant or Duck. Miami could leave them out of this week’s game to give them two more weeks of preparation before their first game of the year.

Players with no game-day designation

Cincinnati’s list includes defensive tackle Jonathan Allen (rest / knee), safety Jordan Battle (hamstring), linebacker Barrett Carter (ankle), defensive tackle B.J. Hill (rest/Achilles), defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence (rest/wrist), and guard Dalton Risner (knee).

item.description: Washington can’t afford to drop to 1-4 overall and 0-3 in the division, making Sunday a key early-season ‘gotta have it’ game

The Daily Slop

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

The Athletic (paywall)

The Cowboys just opened the door for the Commanders, but Washington must make it count

The Commanders are 1-3 and currently sit at the bottom of the division, but their fortune could change drastically when they host the New York Giants (3-1) on Sunday.

“It is wide open, you saw that,” Commanders general manager Adam Peters said during his weekly paid appearance on 106.7 The Fan on Friday. “I think this is one of those divisions that’s going to go down to the end. If we get this win on Sunday, we’re right back in it. But we’ve got to handle our business.”

Working in the team’s favor this week is the return of quarterback Jayden Daniels, who will start after missing the last two games because of an elbow dislocation. Daniels will wear a motion-restriction brace that will keep his left (non-throwing) arm from extending fully.

Getting the tight ends involved more in the pass game will be essential if Washington is without not just Stefon Diggs, who was ruled out Friday, but also Terry McLaurin. The two receivers are dealing with hamstring injuries they suffered in London. McLaurin did not play against the Colts, but practiced Friday and is questionable to play against the Giants.

[T]he Commanders’ have a chance to redirect their future on Sunday.

Commanders Rule Out Six Players, Leave Major Terry McLaurin Question Unanswered

The Washington Commanders will enter Sunday’s game without six players: WR Stefon Diggs (hamstring), Marcus Mariota (knee), Percy Butler (hamstring), Nick Cross (illness), Charles Omenihu (groin/ankle), and Tyler Owens (hamstring) will all be out after missing Friday’s practice. Diggs is obviously the biggest name on the list, but four defensive players, including three safeties, will be out against the Giants.

Since the first injury report came out on Wednesday, everyone has been worried that both Diggs and Terry McLaurin would miss this week’s game. McLaurin is now officially listed as questionable after returning to limited participation in practice Friday. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn stopped short of confirming McLaurin would play Sunday when he spoke Friday afternoon: “Terry, I thought, looked really good today.” Quinn added that the team would decide on McLaurin closer to game time.

The Commanders will get Jayden Daniels, Sam Cosmi, and Rachaad White back this week. Daniels was a full participant in practice every day, clearing the checkpoint Quinn established last week. Jayden Daniels gives Washington a chance of getting its season back on track, but there are other issues to resolve

the NFC East is far from a juggernaut division. The Giants are currently the top team, but there’s plenty of reason to doubt their ability to sustain their level of play.

New York will be without quarterback Jaxson Dart and outside linebacker Brian Burns for the rest of the season. The last two teams they’ve beaten — the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals — are a combined 1-7.

Kaytron Allen was claimed off of waivers by the Dolphins

Running back Kaytron Allen was claimed by the Miami Dolphins on Friday afternoon, exactly one day after the Washington Commanders opted to waive the rookie. Allen also became the first roster cut casualty from the 2026 draft class as Allen arrived in Washington as one of two picks in the sixth round, but now adds a question mark for a front office that entered the draft with limited capital to work with.

Allen also heads to a team that is already familiar with him given the rookie rushed for 85 yards and one touchdown against the Dolphins in the preseason opening win for an encouraging NFL debut. The rookie now heads to a backfield that saw De’Von Achane already go down with a season ending ACL injury, while he joins Ollie Gordon, Jaylen Wright and Carlos Washington in the week five.

Riggo’s Rag

7 Commanders players under pressure to deliver this Sunday

Treylon Burks – Commanders WR

Stefon Diggs won’t feature against the New York Giants with a hamstring injury. Terry McLaurin is trending in the right direction, but even if he does get the green light, the wide receiver will not be at 100 percent.

The Commanders have Jayden Daniels and Sam Cosmi back, which is something. But without Diggs and McLaurin not at full health, others have to step up.

Treylon Burks should get the first shot at becoming a prominent feature in the team’s offensive strategy. He’s always had the talent; consistency is the biggest stumbling block. The Commanders believed enough in the wideout to give him a new one-year deal this offseason, but he’s caught only three passes on six targets this season.

However, two of those have gone for touchdowns. Burks is a big-play waiting to happen, and he needs to show these qualities more often without Diggs to lean on.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt – Commanders RB

The Commanders need to get the run game going. It’s been underwhelming so far, and the situation involving sixth-round rookie Kaytron Allen has placed more scrutiny on Adam Peters’ thought process.

Washington placed faith in experience over development, a trap they fell into last season with little success. It’ll be interesting to see how the dynamic shakes out from here, but there is no questioning the need for Jacory Croskey-Merritt to make more of an impression.

Croskey-Merritt has lost momentum after his surprising rookie surge. He’s been careless with the football, and he hasn’t attacked gaps with the same conviction over four weeks. Austin Ekeler looked like Washington’s best running back in Week 4, and he’d only been back with the franchise for a few days before getting involved.

Commanders Scouting Report: How Washington Exploits Jameis Winston’s Penchant for Mistakes

Winston is an old bird among a league of younglings, but he showed last weekend he still has some of that gunslinger mentality, going 18-of-29 for 250 yards and tossing three touchdowns and two interceptions; it brought back memories of his 30/30 season of 2019 in Tampa Bay. I couldn’t get much out of his film in the Tennessee game; the matchup was played during a nor’easter, and the weather was a major factor. One constant: teams were able to get at him, as he was sacked seven times across his two starts.

Isaiah Likely Tests Washington’s Tight End Coverage

In his two starts, Winston has targeted TE Isaiah Likely the most (17); Likely caught seven of those for 66 yards last weekend, leading the Giants in receptions against Arizona. With opposing tight ends acting like a thorn in the franchise’s side for what seems like forever, Likely is the name to watch on Sunday, especially if Malik Nabers doesn’t play (he was limited Thursday). Nabers has done well with Winston, catching 11 passes (13 targets) for 138 yards and a touchdown.

Washington has to find a way to get after Winston, who is susceptible to the pass rush and makes mistakes often. If they don’t, Winston could have a field day with the weapons New York brings to the table. Isaiah Likely is a nightmare in the red zone, and Washington is a train wreck trying to stop tight ends in that section of the field. The Commanders must find a way to eliminate the chance of it happening altogether, since stopping it seems futile.

Commanders.com

3 keys to Commanders vs. Giants

Shut down the run game

The Giants are going to run the ball on Sunday, regardless of whether the Commanders can bring pressure. They’re near the bottom of the league in yards per attempt but seventh in rushing attempts. They’re committed to leaning on Cam Skattebo, who paces their ground attack and is tied with Isaiah Likely for the most first downs generated on the team.

The Commanders, however, have one of the stingiest defenses against the run. They’ve allowed the fourth-fewest rushing first downs all season, and it doesn’t take long for teams to get the message that they won’t have success on the ground. The Commanders’ defense has only seen 94 rushing attempts — the sixth-fewest in the league.

Washington has solid run defenders at the line of scrimmage — Javon Kinlaw is 10th in run stop win rate — but the secret to their success is the linebacker position. Rookie Sonny Styles is third on the team in tackles, while players like Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson help set edges to prevent runs from getting to the sideline.

The key for the Commanders will be to get Skattebo down as quickly as possible. He’s ninth in yards after contact but only has three broken tackles so far this season. If they can do that, it’ll force the Giants into longer third-down scenarios — an area where the Giants are top 10 but faced distances of five yards or fewer on nine of their 15 attempts against the Arizona Cardinals last week.

NFL defensive rookie rankings at quarter mark of 2026 season: Sonny Styles or Arvell Reese at No. 1?

This rookie crop is absolutely LOADED at linebacker.

I’m talking about the off-ball types. They don’t typically move the needle in pre-draft hype, though this past cycle was different, with a pair of freakish Ohio State products garnering ample attention before ultimately coming off the board as top-10 picks. Those two have hit the ground running (and hitting), making them the easiest selections for this ranking. But they’re not the only LBs who’ve tickled my fancy in the first month of the season. In fact, the position offers so many viable candidates for praise that I had to make some painful omissions (sorry, Jaishawn Barham and Harold Perkins Jr.) to prevent this file from becoming a pure list o’ linebackers.

Not that the other defensive positions are devoid of fresh intrigue — though there does seem to be a shortage of game wreckers up front, at least in the early goings — but the ‘backers have made an indelible mark in the first quarter of the 2026 campaign. Consequently, they dominate this premature rundown of the 10 best defensive rookies, starting at the top with those two aforementioned Buckeyes.

Rank 1 – Sonny Styles – WAS – LB

DRAFTED: Round 1, No. 7 overall

Styles doesn’t have the best stats among rookie defenders, but it sure feels like he’s popped the most. He announced his arrival with a vengeance in Week 1, absolutely bulldozing Saquon Barkley en route to a sack. Two weeks later, he played a critical role in Washington’s shocking upset of the Super Bowl champion Seahawks, earning NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors after racking up five tackles, a QB hit, two pass breakups, a forced fumble and an interception. That kind of well-rounded production suits the versatile 6-foot-5, 243-pounder, who spent his first two years at Ohio State as a safety before converting to linebacker. With injuries in Washington’s linebacking corps, Styles has been forced to wear the green dot at times, and the 21-year-old has capably organized Dan Quinn’s defense. At this point, I’m not sure what Styles can’t do.

The Cowboys’ defense is making no progress. It might be worse than last year

Several times over the last three months, Jerry Jones has made comments, sometimes in jest, about the Dallas Cowboys’ defense being better this year because it can’t be any worse than last year.

Five games in, Jones can’t be too sure about that any more.

Facing an undrafted rookie quarterback making his second start for a winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers team, the Cowboys suffered a stunning 24-16 loss Thursday night at AT&T Stadium.

5 plays that cost the Cowboys vs. the Buccaneers

Once again, they failed to limit explosive plays. If the Tampa Bay Buccaneers wanted to gash them on the ground, they could. If they wanted to exploit them through the passing game, no problemo. This defense is a rudderless ship that cannot get out of its own way.

As for the offense that was tabbed the Greatest Offense There Is (GOTI), not so fast either. The offense led by Dak Prescott was lifeless in the first half. Prescott was far from his normal self, and the offense paid dearly for it.

Eagles vs. Jaguars: Three must-know storylines for NFL Week 5 London game

The road forward starts on Sunday against a Jaguars defense, led by DC Anthony Campanile, that has stymied opponents this season. Jacksonville has accumulated 41 pressures without blitzing (tied for fifth in the NFL, per Next Gen Stats), while Philly’s O-line, as previously constructed, allowed 12 sacks (fourth-most) and a 43.2% pressure rate (third-highest, per NGS).

Big Blue View

Giants-Commanders matchup: Can the Giants contain QB Jayden Daniels?

How to play a Daniels-led offense?

This is, of course, the question facing the Giants this week.

We saw just how much faster and just plain better the Giants played in the final three quarters against the Cardinals. Playing press-man coverage, mixing pressure looks, and attacking the offense ignited the Giants’ defense and allowed them to smother a talented Cardinals’ offense.

The X-factor in all this is Daniels and his legs. Daniels is a talented passer, but his mobility is what maximizes his arm talent. The question the Giants will have to answer is just how mobile Daniels will be. Playing pressure defense and attacking gaps creates opportunities for mobile quarterbacks. Missed or evaded tackle attempts are opportunities to scramble and extend plays, or pick up yards on the ground. Likewise, man coverage plays to the Giants’ strengths in the secondary, however that also takes eyes out of the backfield and makes the secondary slower to react to quarterback runs.

The answer has traditionally been to spy the quarterback, and that’s a viable route for the Giants. The duo of Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese are among the longest and most athletic linebacker duos in the NFL. They can cover a lot of ground, and are secure tackles when they arrive. That could make them effective counters against Daniels on the ground.

Taking things a step further, Wilson could make use of simulated pressures. Walking Reese, Edmunds, or both, up to the A or B-gaps to show pressure before backing them off into coverage will help to muddy Daniels’ reads and confuse their battered offensive line’s protection calls.

Likewise, a Fire Zone blitz that sends a fifth rusher but creates a layered defense behind the pressure could give the Giants the ability to use their athletic rushers without compromising their ability to cover behind it. Mixing simulated pressures, smart blitzes, and Green Dog (ie: a blitzer only rushing if a running back stays in to pass protect) blitzes could help keep Washington off balance while playing to the Giants’ strengths.

The Giants’ defense is obviously better when they’re using their speed and being aggressive. However, they also need to do so in ways that don’t allow Washington to pick up easy yards.

Using their athleticism to disrupt Washington’s offense without creating opportunities for easy yards is a knife-edge line for the Giants to walk. But a win could depend on it, as they can’t allow Daniels to get comfortable, nor can they allow him to run wild.

Washington Commanders vs New York Giants Week 5: Five Questions with Big Blue View

How precarious is the Giants’ hold on the lead in the NFC East?

A lot of the Giants’ season is going to revolve around QB Jameis Winston and his ability to fill in for Jaxson Dart. What have you seen out of Jameis so far, and what do you think about what he brings to the table vs JJ McCarthy?

Jameis is Jameis. He was fantastic at times against the Cardinals, mystifyingly bad at other times. That’s how you throw for 250 yards with 3 TDs and 2 INTs. I’m going to discount Week 3 against Tennessee because that game was played in rain and high winds with gusts nearing 40 mph. He did not turn the ball over and the Giants won, despite not scoring a touchdown. So, you live with it.

Jameis brings experience and leadership. He was named to the team’s Leadership Council and voted as a team captain long before Dart was injured. How many backup quarterbacks are voted as a captain by teammates? [Bill-in-Bangkok: As it turns out, both teams involved in this game. Injured backup Marcus Mariota was put forward as captain by his teammates prior to the Week 3 home game vs Seattle] If the Giants win enough games, it is going to be hard for John Harbaugh to justify replacing Winston with McCarthy. That said, if Winston’s turnovers hold the Giants back Harbaugh won’t hesitate to go to McCarthy.

Nobody really knows what the Giants will get out of McCarthy if and when he plays, but Harbaugh won’t sit around and watch the season go down the drain because Winston can’t, or won’t, protect the football.

Arvell Reese vs. Sonny Styles: Which rookie linebacker has been, will be, better?

Nick Baumgardner (draft analyst, The Athletic)

“I think both Reese and Styles are playing really well right now, improving with each week. Styles is probably a tick ahead as a coverage defender right now and while he’s been slightly more productive as a pass rusher, it’s important to remember a few things. The Giants started Reese, a younger player, at a position (stack LB) where he was sort of part-time last season. He’s needed a bit more time to adjust there as Styles is simply playing the spot he had in college.

“Long-term, I still think Reese is going to be the more impactful front-seven defender. Styles, however, has an elite coverage ceiling. We’ve already seen a bit of that from Dan Quinn and the Commanders. And, remember: Styles used to be a safety in college. That piece is more natural for him. Whereas rushing the passer and stopping the run is where Reese will ultimately thrive.”

item.title: Sean McVay should never give up playcalling
item.description: Sean Payton and DeMeco Ryans take back playcalling duties. Sean McVay should never give it up.
item.content:encoded:
Sean Payton and DeMeco Ryans spent the last few days unwinding the exact decision that Sean McVay has refused to make. The head coaches of the Denver Broncos and Houston Texans took playcalling duties back from their coordinators after early-season struggles.

The lesson for the Los Angeles Rams is simple: don’t create an unnecessary problem you then must fix in October.

Payton handed the Broncos’ offensive keys to Davis Webb in an effort to retain the rising star on the coaching staff. Denver is now 2-2 after making the AFC Championship game last season. Quarterback Bo Nix has just five touchdowns and three interceptions. On Thursday Payton said, “We’ll make a change offensively; I’ll call the plays.” He framed it as instincts and experience. Webb, who last offseason was on the cusp of the head coaching ranks, is now directionless.

In Houston, Ryans took defensive playcalling back from Matt Burke following a winless start after four weeks. The Texans were one of the NFL’s best defenses over the last two years. So far they look nothing like themselves. Communication lapses and production worse than their talent level are the main culprits. Burke actually took playcalling responsibilities from Ryans last year after a similar 0-3 start. This year the script has flipped.

But does it really matter which man pulls the strings? Teams cannot change schemes overnight. The selection might vary, but the menu is largely still the same. Even if head coaches are not the primary playcaller, they still provide significant input throughout the game. It’s likely a role that garners far more media coverage than it deserves.

NFL franchises are not coaching factories. Would it be a positive for the Broncos or Texans if their hot shot coordinators eventually join the head coaching ranks? Of course. Bad teams rarely see their coaches leave for promotions. Greener pastures also help recruit new talent.

The Rams don’t pay Sean McVay around $15M annually because he is adept at developing coaches for other teams. They fork over the big bucks because he gives his offense an edge through his scheme and calling the right plays at the right time. Handing over the duties to Nate Scheelhaase because he’s on the head coaching radar would be silly, even if Scheelhaase leaving would net the team two future third-round picks.

Payton and Ryans are admitting—very publicly—that the title of head coach does not require surrendering the thing you’re best at. Payton has been a playcaller for the better part of two decades. Ryans built his reputation as a defensive mind. They tried to outsource the job, watched the product suffer, and reclaimed it. That is not emulation. It’s damage control.

No one wants to see an emulation of McVay calling plays. We deserve the real thing.

And we will probably get it for a while longer. Sean McVay shouldn’t and likely won’t give up playcalling after watching the very public and recent discourse surrounding Sean Payton and DeMeco Ryans.

item.title: Ultimate Fan: Broncos need to get back in sync
item.description: Well, ultimate Broncos fans, the football gods were definitely Niners fans last week, but that’s OK, no one is truly a Chargers fan so all should be right with the world in a few days.
