item.content:encoded:
Well, ultimate Broncos fans, the football gods were definitely Niners fans last week, but that’s OK, no one is truly a Chargers fan so all should be right with the world in a few days.

And helping the Broncos get back to winning ways is a veteran to the UFG — SickBoy67 — who is feeling like most of us…excited for the potential every week but frustrated by slow starts and squandered opportunities.

Here’s to reversing that on a road game that always feels like home. And as always, come for the great insight and analysis on the UFG, stay for the superb “favorites” and “why I am a Broncos fan” … always the best stuff here!

Week 5: Broncos at Chargers

MHR – The Niners outcome wasn’t necessarily unexpected given the challenge, but it was certainly a disappointing result. What are your overall thoughts on the game?
SickBoy67: I wasn’t expecting a win, but I was hoping for a closely fought game. The team managed that in the first half, but things slipped away after that. I think I feel the same frustration that most fans feel. I’m sick of the slow starts, and I’d like to see this team play a complete game at the level of competence and intensity that we know they’re capable of.

MHR – Sean Payton announced Thursday that he would be taking over play calling. What do you think of this change…good idea? Not great? Doesn’t really matter?
SickBoy67: I’m disappointed that Webb is only being given four games, but at the same time, windows close quickly in the NFL and the margins are thin. I can’t say whether things would have been different if Payton had called every game this year because this team has been notorious for slow starts during his time in Denver. We also have to consider the quality of the defenses the team has faced so far. I guess we’ll see how the team responds in the next couple of weeks.

MHR – The slow starts keep coming up. Payton says it isn’t a script problem, it’s the little details, and Courtland Sutton said the offense has to tighten up its attention to detail. How frustrated are you with the slow starts, and what has to change on that opening drive Sunday? Do the Broncos get on the board first?
SickBoy67: They have to be more effective running the ball, and they have to commit to doing it early. Tampa had an 11 minute opening drive last night. That wears a defense down. As to why it hasn’t been working, I think pretty much every coach and player on offense, with the possible exceptions of Harvey and Bryant, have mud on their hands.

MHR – Bo Nix has been the comeback guy but has also had some costly turnovers. This week he faces a Chargers defense that forced five turnovers against Buffalo and still lost the game. Nix says he doesn’t have to be a hero on every play. How confident are you that he takes what the defense gives him and protects the ball?
SickBoy67: I’m fairly confident about this aspect of Bo’s game. He’s usually pretty good at protecting the ball and being risk averse. A pretty good argument can be made that he’s been too cautious this year. He hasn’t found his rhythm yet and he often doesn’t look comfortable. 

MHR – Payton’s keys for the offense were an efficient run game, play action, and early-down success, meaning no more third-and-long. He also called J.K. Dobbins an important piece. Is the run game ready to show up this week? Which back needs to have the biggest day on Sunday?
SickBoy67: Well, it would be Dobbins for sure. Harvey has improved as a runner, but he still doesn’t have the best vision for holes. He’s an amazing weapon in space, though. That really leaves Dobbins to do the heavy lifting. So far this season, he hasn’t looked right. I think he’s got some lingering injury issues which are slowing him down. I’m not sure this team will look dramatically better this week, but the Chargers run defense isn’t as scary as some we’ve faced, so there’s always hope.

MHR –  RJ Harvey had 10 catches last week while Sutton had one. This was partly due to the soft-zone defense, according to the head coach. Do you think it’s a problem that the ball isn’t necessarily getting to our biggest playmakers that often, such as Sutton and Jaylen Waddle? What kind of balance would you like to see between the run and pass game on Sunday and does it matter who is catching the ball?
SickBoy67: It’s definitely a problem, but it goes back to taking what the defense gives us. If the running game is ineffective, defenses can put more players into coverage. Then they can play the Fangio zone philosophy of allowing short passes and waiting for the offense to get impatient or make a mistake. We need more balance in the passing game, but that starts having a more effective running game. 

MHR – In a bit of a surprise, the Chargers are averaging just 16.8 points a game through four games, so this could be a lower-scoring game. Last year the Chargers rallied from a late double-digit deficit to beat the Broncos 23-20 at SoFi, and the Broncos have struggled to close out games in their last two road matchups with the Chargers. Now they face a winless, desperate team. Will this be a defensive battle, a come-from-behind surge by the Broncos to get a win or should the Broncos dominate this one?
SickBoy67: I think this will be a defensive battle because I expect our defense to play well and our offense to continue to have a slow start. I think that they will come alive in the second half, as is usually the case, and pile on the points, though.

MHR – Justin Herbert has been sacked 12 times in four games, and injuries forced the Chargers to play four rookies on the offensive line against Seattle. Is this the Sunday the Broncos’ pass rush really shows up (finally)?
SickBoy67: Yes. If there’s one unit that will have a ‘get right’ game this week, it’s the pass rushers. My one concern is the corners covering well enough to buy them the time to get home. It’s not that I don’t have confidence in Barron or Abrams-Draine, it’s more that they’re a bit of an unknown commodity as starting boundary corners.

MHR – Herbert has also thrown six interceptions to four touchdown passes this season, and Payton raved about young corners Kris Abrams-Draine and Jahdae Barron for their instincts while Riley Moss and Pat Surtain II are out with injury. Who gets the Broncos’ first takeaway Sunday? How many picks will Herbert throw this week?
SickBoy67: Again, we have to see how they do, but my bet would be McMillian or Huff, anyway. Both of these guys have a penchant for impact plays, and Hufanga has learned to catch the football, it seems.

MHR – Payton compared McDaniel’s offense to Kyle Shanahan’s, and the Broncos just faced Shanahan’s 49ers. But the Chargers are 0-4, so how worried are you that McDaniel attacks this Vance Joseph’s defense the same way he did with the Dolphins in 2023? What is the best way for the Broncos’ defense to keep Justin Herbert in check?
SickBoy67: I’d be fine with him attacking it the same way because I think it would blow up in his face. In 2023, Vance was trying to marry his system with a lot of the verbiage and concepts of the Fangio system in order to make the players more comfortable. He admitted afterwards that it was a huge mistake because it had the opposite effect. Although the defense has taken a step backward so far this season, they are a more talented and accomplished unit than the one McDaniel faced in 2023.

MHR – Which Chargers offensive player scares you the most –  Herbert, Ladd McConkey or Quentin Johnston through the air, or the running back committee?
SickBoy67: McConkey. He just always seems to be open and to make a big play when they need one. It’s possible that he won’t play this week, so that should make life a bit easier.

MHR – Which ONE player on offense and ONE player on defense has to be an MVP on Sunday for the Broncos?
SickBoy67: On offense, I’m just going to say Bo. He needs to settle down and be comfortable out there. If he does that, I think things will be okay on offense even if the running game comes up short. On defense, I think it’s Hufanga. He makes a lot of things happen in the secondary. If he plays lights out, it will be long day for Herbert and that offense.

MHR – What is one word to describe the season so far? What one word do you hope describes it the rest of the season?
SickBoy67: So far, I would say out of sync. Not one word, but one idea. For the rest of the season, I’m hoping for balance. If this team has balance, they can beat anyone.

item.title: Detroit Lions vs. Arizona Cardinals preview: 3 key stats
item.description: A data-driven preview of Lions at Cardinals, focusing on key stats and matchups.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions had started at least 4-1 in each of the previous three seasons. Leading the NFC North pack from the jump was starting to become the norm. Not only have they suffered their earliest second loss since 2022, but both losses came in utterly demoralizing and shocking primetime fashion. Now they appear to be a team that has lost respect nationally and around the league, a month into the season without having played anything close to a complete game.

It was one of the most unenthusiastic weeks to be a Lions fan in recent years following the Bryce Young buzzsaw they ran into in Charlotte. Now they’ll head to the desert to take on the younger LaFleur brother, Mike, needing a get-right victory and a complete four-quarter performance to inspire some hope for the season heading into the much-needed early Week 6 bye. They’ll do so riding a 5-1 record against the Cardinals since 2017, after the Ford family’s franchise went 0-7 in seven matchups with Arizona between 2006 and 2015.

The Cardinals have invested heavily in their skill players, with Trey McBride, Michael Wilson, Jeremiyah Love, and Marvin Harrison Jr., and all eyes will be on the Lions defense fighting back and moving past the narrative that they’re the worst defense in all of football. Every team in football has warts right now, so let’s get into my three key stats and matchups for Sunday afternoon’s West Coast business trip and how the Lions can rid themselves of those warts.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus.

Three TEs is a Crowd

While the Detroit Lions defense has been inexplicably dysfunctional this season, one thing they haven’t been on a bus straight to Rock Bottom on is defending against 13-personnel. Despite struggling overall in run defense against the Bills and Panthers, they’ve found some success against three tight end sets, allowing only 3.31 yards per rush on 16 attempts, with just one explosive rush allowed.

Even against 13-personnel as a pass defense, where the Lions typically match with their base defense, they’ve been effective, allowing 10-of-17 passing (58.8% completion percentage) for 102 yards (6.0 yards per attempt, 12th), a 41.2% success rate (14th), 4.9 yards per catch (13th), and a 5.9% explosive pass rate (14th). All respectable numbers. If they could simply be middle of the pack in most pass-defense metrics, the outlook for their season would be a lot more optimistic than it’s felt in the aftermath of the last two dreary defeats. Most promisingly, the Lions’ pass rush against 13-personnel has generated a 66.7% pressure rate (3rd) and a 9.5% sack rate (8th).

Their 13-personnel defensive prowess is important when facing the Cardinals in a post-Drew Petzing world. While Arizona’s 12-personnel usage has sharply declined from 36.2% (3rd) last season to 14.8% under LaFleur, its 13-personnel usage has remained a priority, jumping from 11.0% in 2025 (3rd) to 20.1% (3rd) when deploying Trey McBride, Elijah Higgins, and Hunter Long (with Tip Reiman injured). [Note: Long was placed on IR this week, with veteran Teagan Quitoriano expected to take his place.]

The Cardinals’ rushing attack from three-tight-end sets has maintained success, averaging 4.14 yards per rush (t-6th), a 47.2% success rate (14th), and +0.02 EPA/rush (10th). They’re also top 10 in both yards before and after contact per carry, with both Jeremiyah Love (47.6% success rate) and Tyler Allgeier (+0.04 EPA/rush) averaging over 4 yards per carry from 13-personnel.

Some of Jacoby Brissett’s best analytical metrics come from his 16 dropbacks (fourth most) when passing out of 13-personnel. He’s 11-for-16 for 90 passing yards (5.6 yards per attempt), two touchdowns, +0.367 EPA/pass (11th), and a 62.5% passing success rate (11th).

While it’s a small sample size, the Lions defense needs to chip away and find avenues where it can have success. Being able to defend well on roughly every fifth play when the Cardinals go to 13-personnel would be a step in the right direction toward getting off the field and holding Arizona to field goals instead of touchdowns in the red zone.

Death by a Thousand Checkdowns

While it’s beneficial for the Lions that Cardinals left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. will miss the game due to injury, leaving either seventh-round rookie Jayden Williams or recently signed Jedrick Wills to man Jacoby Brissett’s blind side, with possibly backup Jon Gaines II filling in for the injury-battling right guard Isaiah Adams, the defense proved Sunday night against the Panthers that a favorable offensive line matchup isn’t always enough.

While Detroit’s defensive front can generate pressure and take advantage of porous offensive lines, the back end hasn’t allowed it to fully capitalize. Receivers were running wide open for easy throws from Bryce Young, who also stood strong in the pocket just long enough to deliver backbreaking completions before the rush could get there. The Cardinals’ passing approach could further mitigate the effectiveness of the Lions’ defensive front against Arizona’s below-average offensive line.

It’s not a dynamic passing attack, instead operating largely on dinking and dunking, which could provide a foundation for the Lions to keep everything in front of them, clean up their short-pass coverage, and maybe even force a hurried mistake.

Among 29 qualifying quarterbacks, Jacoby Brissett ranks last in yards per pass attempt (5.4), 27th in average depth of target (6.10 yards) and average time to throw (2.6 seconds), and 26th in deep-ball rate (5.9% on throws of 20-plus air yards). He’s also tied with Joe Burrow for the second-most throws in under 2.5 seconds (94).

All pedestrian and manageable numbers. The Cardinals’ passing offense is by far the least explosive in the league, averaging an explosive pass rate of only 2.6%. The next closest is the Giants at 6.2% (31st), while Arizona’s rushing offense isn’t much better, also ranking last with a 5.6% explosive run rate.

The Lions defense ranks bottom five in both explosive pass and run rate allowed, but maybe this Cardinals offensive bunch is one against which they can finally look like a decently taught and executed defense, with all 11 players on the same page and where they need to be. Dan Campbell mentioned the need for his defensive players to be more disciplined this week and also said, “I want our guys to be where they’re supposed to be when they’re supposed to be there.”

Perhaps this Cardinals offense is the starter kit Detroit needs to build back toward being bend-but-don’t-break as opposed to simply being broken.

Finding Their Roar

Drew Petzing should be all too familiar with his former co-worker, Cardinals fourth-year defensive coordinator Nick Rallis, someone who makes chicken salad out of chicken shit with disguised blitzes and simulated pressures. Petzing’s offensive unit has managed to put up points every game, but it hasn’t been as consistent or had as cohesive an approach throughout a game as one would like given its talent.

Dan Campbell challenged the offense during multiple media availabilities this week.

“We’re not going to be average. We’re going to raise the floor on these guys. Man, we’re going to push them,” Campbell said on local radio. “We’ve got too much offensively right now. Our quarterback’s too good. Our playmakers are too good. And we’ve got a young, hungry offensive line that’s got a ton of room to grow.”

Petzing, in what some might call a revenge game against a talent-deficient Cardinals defense, will look to put together his most complete game plan of the season.

The Cardinals’ defensive front has some solid players in Josh Sweat, Darius Robinson, edge-setter Zaven Collins, promising young defensive tackle Walter Nolen Jr., and imposing old friend Roy Lopez. Much like the Lions defense last week, it’s the Cardinals’ spine of the defense, led by 10-year veteran Budda Baker, fellow safety Andrew Wingard (ruled out this week), and linebackers Mack Wilson Sr. and Jack Gibbens, that the Lions offense could exploit.

While the Lions’ third-down offense has been middle of the pack by most metrics, one of the Cardinals’ two glaring defensive weaknesses is getting off the field on third down, where they’re allowing a 47.7% conversion rate (26th) and +0.698 EPA/play (32nd). The Cardinals are also getting bombarded allowing a league-worst 12.7% explosive pass rate.

The Lions need to continue striving for better results on early downs, but against the Cardinals, they can dominate possession of the football and keep their defense off the field by finding more success moving the chains on third down and generating chunk plays through Jared Goff’s bevy of weapons in the passing game.

item.title: Giants notebook: Abdul Carter, Ben Mann’s accuracy, more
item.description: News, notes, numbers to know before Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Here are some notes, quotes, and numbers to know before the New York Giants face the Washington Commanders on Sunday.

Confounding Carter

Abdul Carter is a confounding pass rusher.

He wins fast:

He wins a lot:

He just does not compile a lot of sacks. He has just one in four games this season, and five in 21 career games.

Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said this week that Carter was “throwing his fastball all game” against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4, and lauded his impact on Arizona quarterback Jacoby Brissett.

It’s hard not to believe the sack numbers will eventually come for Carter.

But, can he play quarterback?

How good has rookie long-snapper Ben Mann been for the Giants this season? This good:

If only Jameis Winston were that accurate.

Unblemished

Commanders coach Dan Quinn is 6-0 as a head coach against the Giants, 4-0 with the Commanders and 2-0 with the Atlanta Falcons, per Giants PR. The only other coach with an undefeated record against the Giants (five-game minimum) is Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams. McVay is 5-0.

Skat’s magic number

In two seasons, the Giants are 5-0 when Cam Skattebo has at least 18 rushing attempts. They are 0-7 when he has 17 carries or fewer.

Speaking of the running game, I wrote this week that coach John Harbaugh admitted the Giants are “just not good enough” in the run game. The longest run from a running back so far this season is 13 yards.

“I think we haven’t fully came into our own yet,” Skattebo said. “I think up front we’re in a new scheme, new system, and these guys are learning. Sisi (offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa) coming in, this is going into game five of his career. The guys up front are learning the system. B-Hud’s (offensive lineman Bryan Hudson) the center now.

“At times, going on, we’ve just got to continue to work and get better at what we’re doing. I think as time goes on, it’s going to get better and better. These guys are going to really find the flow in the system and things are going to be just fine.”

The most interesting takeaway there is Skattebo revealing that Hudson has indeed taken the starting center job from John Michael Schmitz.

On the flip side, this is the first time since 2006 that the Giants have not allowed at least one run of 25 yards through their first four games.

(H/T, Giants PR)

Dealing with Jayden

The Giants have to approach Jayden Daniels, a quarterback who can be devastating when he begins to run, differently than the stationary Jacoby Brissett of the Arizona Cardinals. Rush discipline is critical.

“That’s a really big thing. That’s a big factor,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “That’s a big challenge because pinning your ears back, what does that exactly mean? There’s lanes, so to speak. There’s leverages. There’s angles involved. I think it’s really important to understand that you’re rushing to the quarterback, not past the blockers or past the offensive line. If you try to rush past the offensive line, you’re usually going to be past the quarterback. That’s not good. So, we want to be to the quarterback in a direct fashion, direct manner. Our guys are really focusing on doing that. But that doesn’t mean you can just run offensive linemen over. They don’t let you do that too often.

“So, you’ve got to have ways to go about getting past them to the quarterback. That’s the challenge. I think if you think about it that way, you can see it’s not the easiest thing in the world to do. But that’s what we work on all the time. We have really good pass rushers, I think it’s starting to heat up a little bit. I feel like you can feel it. So, it’s good.”

item.title: 5 Questions with the Enemy: Drew Petzing’s return, the struggling Lions defense and more
item.description: Talking about the Detroit Lions before their matchup with the Arizona Cardinals.
item.content:encoded:
Happy Saturday one and all.

The Arizona Cardinals take on the Detroit Lions and Ryan Mathews of Pride of Detroit was kind enough to answer some questions for us ahead of the matchup.

Enjoy.

Right or wrong Arizona Cardinals fans were excited for the Drew Petzing era to end… what do the Lions fans think after four games?

Aside from the “Lions miss Ben Johnson” memes, Detroit’s offense has looked progressively more potent each week. Detroit is fifth in points per game (29.8), sixth in yards per game (389.3), and seventh in EPA/play (+0.10). Things were a bit uneven in Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints, but the Lions capitalized on a couple of turnovers, turning a short field into touchdowns. Detroit put up 31 points in three consecutive weeks, but last week against the Carolina Panthers, the Lions’ offense stalled out in the red zone a couple of times, settling for field goals instead of touchdowns—something that hadn’t been an issue prior to “Sunday Night Football;” Detroit had a 78.6% red zone conversion rate heading into Week 4, good for sixth in the NFL.

It does still feel like there’s another dimension of this offense to be unlocked, namely the explosive plays. It’s not necessarily for a lack of trying, as there’s been some failure to execute on those plays be it drops, errant throws, or breakdowns in pass protection. Once Detroit is able to break off some big runs or connect on some more of these deep shots, the offense will feel like it’s back to being one of the most lethal units in the NFL.

 What on earth is going on with the Lions defense?

It’s a fool’s errand to make sense of why this defense has been as bad as it’s been through four weeks. The defensive line is legitimately good. Alim McNeill is first among interior defenders in pressures (20), Aidan Hutchinson is tied for first in pressures (29) among edge defenders, and Tyleik Williams has played really well against the run in his second year out of Ohio State.

But for as good as the defensive front has been, the back-seven has been a disaster. Detroit’s 109.3 net passing yards allowed per game when getting pressure is the worst in the NFL—the team ranked 31st, the Atlanta Falcons, allow just 65.3 net passing yards when getting pressure. Woof.

Last week’s performance really boiled down to the poor preparation for Carolina. The Panthers RPO’d the Lions into oblivion, with Bryce Young identifying the blitz and throwing the ball to the vacated part of the field. The cornerbacks are playing off coverage often, something that wasn’t a staple during the Aaron Glenn era, and it just doesn’t make sense given how much pressure their defensive front is generating (39.3%, ninth in the NFL). Some of that has to do with the personnel deficiencies—Detroit was in on the Joey Porter Jr. sweepstakes—but some of it is asking a veteran safety like Chuck Clark to pull off feats of athleticism he just can’t make happen at this point in his career. Dan Campbell is adamant there’s more tinkering that can be done to fix things, but consider me skeptical.

The Arizona Cardinals defense can’t stop a cold, so is this the week the Lions put up 40+ for the first time?

That sure would be nice! It would take Detroit to start hitting on those explosive plays that have yet to materialize reliably. Arizona’s run defense is second best in EPA/rush (-0.24) and they sport a better than average stuff rate at 17.0% (t-13th). The Lions need their rushing offense to be more consistent from kickoff in order to throw up 40+ points in the desert. It helps keep them on schedule and ahead of the sticks, which, at risk of sounding cliche, is when this offense really thrives. Especially with this defense looking the way it does, it’s important this offense put together long, sustained drives to wear down their opponent and their own defense off the field.

Do you feel like Dan Campbell is on the hot seat?

Not whatsoever. It’s really interesting to get that question from you, and to think of the way things look from the outside looking in. Detroit finished 15-2 just two seasons ago, backslid to a 9-8 record a year ago, and things aren’t off to the hottest of starts, but Campbell’s status with the team, that’s not even really a conversation until this team’s season plays out. It’s dependent upon their record, the playoffs, and a lot more. It would take a pretty abysmal finish to this season for Campbell’s job to be considered at risk.

The Cardinals are not covering the 4.5-point line, at least in my mind, but do the Lions do enough on defense to get under 53.5, or is this going to be a monster total?

Drew Petzing revenge game incoming?

There’s no reason to believe this Lions defense can prevent teams from putting up at least 21 points in a game, so yes, this game feels like it has a great chance at reaching the over. Add to the fact that Campbell has been incredibly vocal about the offense not accepting “mediocrity” this week, noting they have too much talent not to expect greatness from that unit, and you could see Detroit’s offense finally exploding for a huge offensive performance. That being said, with the way Detroit’s defense has looked in 14 of its past 16 quarters, this will likely be a one-score game when it’s all said and done.

item.title: Bills trending up, trending down: Who Bills need on Monday Night Football in Los Angeles
item.description: Which Bills are rising/falling with a Week 5 tough challenge against the Rams ahead?
item.content:encoded:
It wasn’t pretty.

The Patriots game told us what’s broken. Monday night at SoFi Stadium tells us whether Buffalo can fix (or at least mask) it in a week. The Rams are 2.5- to 3-point favorites, and they’re bringing the one thing the Bills’ secondary has struggled most to stop: receivers who win on the outside.

I’m not here to relitigate the 29-26 loss. I’m here to use it. Every Hero and Head Scratcher below is judged by what he showed against New England and what he has to do against Matthew Stafford, Puka Nacua, and Davante Adams.

Here’s the big picture. Buffalo’s offense leads the league in scoring (127 points through four games) and converts 53.3% of its third downs. The Rams’ defense allows just 145.5 passing yards per game and a 75.4 passer rating. On the other side, Buffalo allows 20.5 passing points per game, the second-most in the league, and a 6.8% touchdown rate (29th), per Sharp Football. A lot of players are banged up. Who needs to step up on the big stage to help the Bills move to 4-1?

Heroes

DE Greg Rousseau: the answer to Stafford’s pocket problem

I’ve tried to avoid repeating names on this list, but it’s impossible at some point. Greg Rousseau has played lights out, week in and week out.

Rousseau has six sacks, the most in the NFL. Against New England, his streak of two sacks per game ended, but he still had eight pressures and at least four hits on Drake Maye, while he defended the run as he usually does, very well. He also had a strip-sack called back after review, in a play where he was an inch away from making it count.

Here’s why Groot matters on Monday. Stafford has the NFL’s third-worst passer rating under pressure (29.1) and the sixth-lowest completion rate when pressured (37.0%). His accuracy is 34 percentage points worse under pressure than in a clean pocket, the largest gap among qualifying quarterbacks. He has already thrown six interceptions in four games (eight all of last year), and he went 32-of-52 for 317 yards, no touchdowns and two picks at Philadelphia. Not exactly MVP numbers.

So the Bills’ best coverage call is to put the heat on Stafford. The catch is real: 4for4 ranks the Rams’ offensive line first in the league, with a 29.5% pressure rate allowed (sixth) and the best interior group at preventing pressure. Rousseau on the edge is Buffalo’s cleanest path to that pocket. With the Bills’ secondary struggling, the pass rush is the plan to save the day.

WR Keon Coleman: Can he be the guy if DJ Moore sits?

DJ Moore left in the second quarter after re-injuring his shoulder and did not practice Thursday. Buffalo has its bye in Week 7, so resting him is a real possibility. Coleman is who stepped up against New England: six catches on seven targets for 116 yards and a touchdown, six of those targets after Moore went out, and the team’s best PFF grade (79.2). In the fourth quarter, he caught a third-and-6 throw for 22, then caught a 24-yarder and a 34-yard touchdown on a deep post to put Buffalo up 26-21. He is 14-for-16 for 217 yards on the season, and with Moore off the field, he has run 3.33 yards per route, per Sharp Football.

Skeptics will say New England was missing its top corner. Fair. The Rams are a different test. Trent McDuffie has allowed only 5 completions on 18 targets (27.8%), and Coleman plays 75% of his snaps outside, though Jaylen Watson is expected to miss the game, which leaves Josh Wallace opposite McDuffie. Los Angeles has allowed just five pass plays of 20-plus yards, tied for the fewest in the league. Buffalo has 17, tied for second most on offense. That’s the matchup: Coleman’s targets against the best secondary in football so far. With Dalton Kincaid and Khalil Shakir also in the fold, Coleman might be able to keep up the good production.

Head Scratchers

CB Maxwell Hairston: from an asset to a liability, to…

Uno was no bueno.

Two touchdowns. Romeo Doubs finished with six catches on nine targets for 58 yards and two scores, both on Hairston, who was the most-targeted defender by New England. On the opening drive, he got lost in zone on a fourth-and-3 conversion, and Doubs beat him on the next play for 14 yards and a touchdown. In the second half, a holding flag wiped out a third-down sack, and two plays later Doubs made a one-handed grab on a 2-yard fade. He also played inexcusably far off the line on a red-zone fourth down. PFF graded him a 32.0, the lowest of any Bill in the game.

This was a regression, not a verdict. Before Sunday, PFF had him at 56.7 on the season, and Next Gen Stats had him allowing a 36.4% completion rate (minimum 10 targets). He’s now at a 114.4 passer rating allowed when targeted, per Sharp Football. Draft status is not a guarantee of professional success, though, and Monday’s receivers don’t care where he was picked.

Adams plays 88% of his snaps outside, and Buffalo allows 9.0 catches per game (26th) and a 9.3% touchdown rate (29th) to outside receivers. His target share has dipped with Nacua back (23.5% of routes and 1.54 yards per route with Nacua on the field, versus 33.5% and 3.23 without), and he saw just four catches for 32 yards in Philadelphia. But he is still touchdown-dependent in this offense, and touchdowns are where Hairston got hurt. Nacua returned from a two-game absence with 9 catches on 12 targets for 125 yards, running a route on 90.7% of dropbacks.

Christian Benford, who missed Week 4 with a toe injury, was back at practice Thursday. But he is not an automatic fix: PFF had him at 40.6 entering Week 4 (97th of 99 corners), and he has allowed a 124.4 passer rating when targeted. Whoever draws Adams and Nacua, the Bills can’t afford a repeat of the fourth-and-short conversions that kept New England’s drives alive.

QB Josh Allen: the last throw can’t be the first problem Monday

I’ll say it plainly: that last throw was a head scratcher. Allen was 23-of-33 for 253 yards, a touchdown and an interception, plus a 2-yard sneak for a score. But down three with the clock on his side, he forced a throw that Craig Woodson picked off to end the game. An inexcusable decision, even if he had his WR open before he had to spin to avoid a sack. It’s a game of inches, and the second he spent to evade the free rusher changed the picture entirely. A 10-year vet, the best QB in the league, can’t do that, period.

He also ran five times for four yards, avoiding contact and looking nothing like himself, mobility-wise. On Thursday, Alen quickly dismissed the possibility of playing injured, but honestly, it’s hard to believe his words with the way he moved last game. Josh has played through some meaningful injuries for a couple of seasons now, and I don’t believe he’s 100% healthy at the moment, as he suggests.

Buffalo has seven giveaways in two games, five against the Chargers and two against New England. The Rams matter here for a specific reason. Their defense is stingy: second in completion rate allowed (53.5%) and first in yards per attempt allowed (4.8). But it isn’t a takeaway machine, and Myles Garrett is on injured reserve, so the pass rush runs through Byron Young (20.1% pressure rate). Allen’s 39.4% play-action rate is second in the NFL, while Stafford’s 22.5% ranks 31st, so Buffalo will lean on the tool this Rams defense has to respect. Establishing the run with James Cook will be important again, and if Buffalo loses Monday, it’s more likely to be because the Bills couldn’t run the ball and gave it away than because the Rams took it.

Honorable Mentions

Trending Up:

  • RB James Cook: 6.4, 6.4, and 6.3 yards per carry over his last three games, and the league’s best rate of 10-plus-yard runs (21.4%). Yet he got just 12 carries on 35 snaps (59%) against New England. The Rams allow 3.8 yards per carry to backs (12th) and a 4.7% rate of 10-plus-yard runs (4th), so he needs volume.
  • DT Greg Gaines: He recovered Maye’s fumble and posted PFF’s third-best grade on the team (73.8). With Ed Oliver sitting out Thursday’s practice with a knee issue, he matters against the NFL’s best interior line at preventing pressure.
  • LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr: Led the defense at 75.9 PFF grade in just 16 snaps (21%). Showed he can add the physicality Terrel Bernard lacks, but also cover, something Dorian Williams has struggled with. Giving him an increase in snaps should help the defense overall.

Trending Down:

  • OT Dion Dawkins: He was responsible for a sack, beaten on a play that could have been a safety, and flagged twice.Byron Young (20.1% pressure rate) is the Rams’ top pass rusher with Garrett on IR.
  • TE Dalton Kincaid: 5-130 and 7-95-1 in Weeks 1 and 2, then 2-38 and 1-7. PFF graded him a 40.2 against New England, with a route rate of 54.3%. He still leads TEs at 3.07 yards per route, but the Rams allow a league-low 2.9 yards per target to tight ends.
  • WR Joshua Palmer: One catch for 3 yards on four targets, a 43.7 PFF grade, and a dropped deep shot. The Rams have allowed only five pass plays of 20-plus yards (tied for fewest), so those downfield chances won’t come often.

FINAL THOUGHTS

Buffalo’s secondary is not going to win this game by itself. It also can’t be the reason Buffalo loses it. If the pass rush gets home on Stafford, if Coleman or Moore is the guy on the outside against McDuffie, and if the Bills stop giving the ball away, the Rams have no good answer for this offense.

I know there are a lot of “ifs”, and the one that bothers me the most wasn’t even mentioned: what if Josh really isn’t healthy? I want his words to be true, and another stellar performance at the SoFi would help a lot with it. Give a healthy Josh Allen a clean pocket and take away the self-inflicted wounds, and I’ll take Buffalo’s best player over anyone else in that building.

Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

item.title: Khalil Mack could return to the Bears
item.description: Eight years after the Bears traded for pass rusher Khalil Mack, the Bears could be doing it all over again.
item.content:encoded:
Eight years after the Bears traded for pass rusher Khalil Mack, the Bears could be doing it all over again.

Via Jonathan Jones of The Athletic (who isn't their "insider" but who is posting a Saturday "insider" column like their former "insider" did), Mack could be making his way back to Chicago before the trade deadline.

The Chargers are 0-4 and fading fast. The Bears are 3-1 and could use a boost on the edge.

Mack has a base salary of $8 million in 2026, the last year of his current deal. He'll have $5.77 million remaining in pay after this week. The Bears, as Jones notes, currently have approximately $9 million in cap space.

Mack, 35, still has gas in the tank. He has three sacks in four games this year, for a team that has yet to enjoy having a late lead that is conducive to the proverbial pinning of the ears back.

If/when the Chargers decide to start moving contracts (they're two games from their bye week), the next question would become compensation for Mack. If he only wants to go to Chicago, that could make it hard to maximize the return.

In 2018, the Bears gave up two first-round picks, a third-round pick, and a sixth-round pick to get Mack. It would be a lot less this time around.

The trade deadline arrives the Tuesday after Week 9. Which is only 31 days away.

item.title: That one time Kyle Shanahan forgot about Jaxon Smith-Njigba
item.description: The 49ers head coach saw the Seahawks receiver at a Pro Day and forgot his name. His GM had to remind him.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are getting ready for Week 5 against the Seattle Seahawks in what is the most important game of the season thus far. If you take the rosters and make a list of the top 10 players between the two of them, Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba would definitely be on that list.

Turns out, he was on Shanahan’s radar for a brief moment in 2021.

During his Friday press conference, Shanahan repeated a story about when he got his first glimpse of Smith-Njigba—when the wide receiver was playing at Ohio State. 2021 was the year the 49ers traded three first-round picks and change to move up to pick No. 3 in the 2021 NFL Draft. While the 49ers ultimately went with Trey Lance, Buckeye quarterback Justin Fields was seen as a distant possibility.

“We were going to Pro Days looking at Fields,” Shanahan recalled. “I just remember that it was a long workout and there was a freshman running all over the place.”

That freshman was Smith-Njigba. Upon seeing the wide receiver, Shanahan might have been less interested in the quarterbacks.

“I just ended up asking [John] Lynch halfway through the end; I was just like, ‘Who the hell is that kid?’ And they’re like, ‘Oh, it’s some freshman.’”

Knowing that was a freshman might have been the end of it. A freshman isn’t going to declare for the draft, and Shanahan’s primary focus was on what quarterback to select from what was (thought at the time) an impressive draft class for the position.

“We got his name and I had forgot the name at the time, like I usually do.”

Smith-Njigba was drafted in the 2023 NFL Draft. There was little Shanahan could have done to snag the player if he wanted to; that was the final year of the 49ers not having a first-round pick due to the Lance trade, and they wouldn’t make a selection in the third round. Their third-round pick, 87th overall, went to safety, Ji’Ayir Brown. You know the 2023 draft as the “Jake Moody Draft,” because he was the next pick of the 49ers, also in the third round.

All Shanahan could do was recall watching him a few years earlier. Lynch pointed out who Smith-Njigba was to Shanahan, and Shanahan didn’t forget.

“He was just running around everywhere, catching everything, and that was extremely impressive.”

item.title: Eagles opposing player to stop, Week 5 edition
item.description: Philadelphia needs their defense to come up big on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles are in freefall right now. They are arguably the biggest disappointment in the NFL this season, along with the Los Angeles Rams, sitting at 2-2 riding a two-game losing streak and getting ready to face the revamped Trevor Lawrence and a very good 3-1 Jacksonville Jaguar team that has given up an AFC-low 53 points this season.

The one benefit Eagles players will have is that the game is not being played at Lincoln Financial Field, where they would hear more venom from the fans on their way to another miserable loss, but rather at 9:30 a.m. ET at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, England.

This past week alone, the Eagles traded away the floundering Cam Jurgens to Baltimore for a 5th round 2027 pick and second-round 2028 pick, and lost all-time great Lane Johnson to retirement. They will be relying on Willie Lampkin to fill in for Jurgens at left guard in his first NFL start, rookie Markel Bell, who played well against the Los Angeles Rams last week, at right tackle, replacing Johnson, and someone no one heard of, Jake Majors making his first career start in place of the injured center Drew Kendall.

So, that means Lampkin and Majors will be making their NFL debuts and Bell will making his NFL second start against a possibly the best defense in the NFL. Not good.

Adding more flame to this combustible mess for the Eagles has been the emergence of Lawrence, who is coming around to look like the quarterback everyone projected him to be as the No.1 pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. He is No. 6 in the NFL in passer rating (111.2), tied for No. 3 overall with 8 touchdown passes, and is averaging 210.8 yards a game passing. On the other side, the Eagles have not yet reached the quarterback, tied for 31st in the league with a scant 4 sacks.

That translates into plenty of time for Lawrence to sit back and shred the Eagles’ passing defense, much like 38-year-old Case “Montana” Keenum did and Rams’ future Hall of Famer Matt Stafford did last week.

Eagles’ defensive coordinator Vic Fangio remains stubborn when it comes to the blitz as a way to stimulate a decent pass rush.

“No, I said I don’t want to blitz until I want to,” he said this week when addressing the media. “Again, it all depends upon the opponent. One of the reasons we played so well the first 10 series was — we weren’t [blitzing] because that quarterback [Stafford] could feast on it.

“They’re really good on offense. The quarterback [Lawrence] is athletic, got a big arm, he’s got a good group of receivers to throw it to. Their running back, 33 [Jacksonville Jaguars RB Bhayshul Tuten] runs really good, kind of a new guy on the scene and they do a good job. They got a very varied running game, a lot of different types of runs, multiple run game and they’re good at it.”

On the other side, Jalen Hurts has more to worry about. For one, it looks like no Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith again, and if anyone thought Hurts was running for his life the first four games of this season, wait until he meets Jacksonville. The Jags are giving up a scant 13.3 points a game, second in the NFL behind Minnesota, and the Eagles are No. 26 in the NFL, averaging as paltry 18.8 points a game.

Add a stubborn, elite defense against an offensive line featuring two starters making their NFL debuts, a shaky offense whose first-year offensive coordinator looks like he is learning as he goes along and a team filled with sagging morale and that brew smells like a recipe for disaster.

It may not only slam the door on the Eagles this Sunday but convince upper management it may be time to start a rebuild.

item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Cleveland Browns

item.content:encoded:
The New York Jets return home on Sunday, looking to avoid their third four-game losing streak in Aaron Glenn’s first 22 games as head coach against the surprising 3-1 Cleveland Browns.

New York has won three of their last four games against Cleveland, including a 27-20 win last season.

Let’s break down the Browns’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

The controversial Deshaun Watson has rebounded from a shaky start to the season to lead the Browns to three straight wins by a total of 10 points. He has a quarterback rating of over 100 and has rushed for 10 first downs.

However, he’s averaging just 214 passing yards per game and has been sacked 11 times with two interceptions and three fumbles.

After going 3-4 as a starter last season, with 10 interceptions, Shedeur Sanders is now back to being the number two.

Sixth round rookie Taylen Green has been the number three, although Dillon Gabriel was activated for practice from injured reserve this week. He will presumably replace Green on the roster soon, but not this weekend.

Offensive Line

The Browns have completely overhauled their starting offensive line since last season. Left tackle Spencer Fano was drafted in the first round and right guard Austin Barber was drafted in the third round, joining three veteran additions as the new starting group.

At right tackle is Tytus Howard, who was acquired via trade. He has five penalties in four games so far this season. The left guard is Zion Johnson, who was a free agency signing who was previously with the Chargers. Center Elgton Jenkins, who will be making his return after missing last Thursday night’s win over the Steelers, was signed in March after his release from the Packers.

The bench at least has a familiar look, as Luke Wypler, Dawand Jones and Teven Jenkins all started games for the Browns last year with Wypler also having started the last game at center. In addition, Zak Zinter has been with the team for three years, although he didn’t start in any of his four appearances last season. All three of his NFL starts were in his rookie year.

(Teven) Jenkins has been ruled out of Sunday’s game but the other offensive lineman on the roster, fifth round rookie Parker Brailsford, will probably still be inactive.

Running Backs

The Browns’ lead back is Quinshon Judkins, who racked up 827 yards and seven touchdowns last season despite only playing in 14 games. He’s off to a bit of a slow start this year, though, as he averages just 3.0 yards per carry.

Raheim Sanders only has six carries as the number two, but he’s used a lot in the passing game and has combined with Judkins for 25 catches in the first four games.

The number three back is Jaleel McLaughlin, who only has two carries this season – although one went for a 28-yard touchdown.

Veteran Michael Burton is also on the roster as a fullback.

Pass catchers

The Browns were surprisingly led in receiving by a rookie last year, as tight end Harold Fannin led the team in catches, yards and touchdown receptions, while 2024 pro bowler Jerry Jeudy had a down year.

Youngsters are leading the way this year too. Second round rookie receiver Denzel Boston leads them in receiving yards and has flashed big play potential with 46 and 55-yard touchdowns as he is dangerous after the catch.

First rounder KC Concepcion has also made an impact and he’s tied with Fannin on 17 receptions to lead the team.

Jeudy has once again made a slow start, but he is still a starter. Backups Isaiah Bond, ex-Jet Malachi Corley and Tylan Wallace have just two catches between them. Wallace is ruled out for Sunday anyway.

Fannin once again leads the Browns with three touchdown catches, but he no longer has David Njoku as a fellow starter at tight end. With seventh round rookie Carsen Ryan ruled out on Sunday, Blake Whiteheart will be the primary backup with Burton perhaps contributing here too. Whiteheart only has two catches this year, but one went for a touchdown.

Defensive Line

The Browns will be shorthanded on the defensive line this weekend, as last year’s first round pick Mason Graham and key reserve Mike Hall were both ruled out. In addition, Kalia Davis – who is on injured reserve but had his practice window opened this week – missed practice on Thursday and Friday so isn’t ready to be activated to provide reinforcements.

Graham had been making a big impact with four sacks in the first four games, so that’s a significant loss.

The starters will now be Maliek Collins and Adin Huntington with two of Cleveland’s three practice squad defensive tackles (Sam Kamara, Chris Williams and Zion Logue) presumably set to be elevated. Collins is a solid player who had 6.5 sacks last year, but the Browns should be downgraded from a unit which was already the ninth-worst in the NFL for yards per attempt allowed.

Cleveland will be at full strength on the defensive line, although Jared Verse hasn’t been very productive so far as he deals with the pressure of being Myles Garrett’s replacement. Verse, who was included in the trade that sent Garrett to the Rams, was a pro bowler last season with 7.5 sacks, but has just two quarterback hits and no sacks so far this season.

The other starting defensive end is Isaiah McGuire with Derek Barnett healthy enough to come off the bench despite missing practice earlier in the week. Sam Williams will also be in the rotation.

The Browns lost a potential starter, Alex Wright, to an Achilles injury in August so he’s out for the year, which is why they added Barnett. Wright had 5.5 sacks last season.

Linebackers

The Browns’ linebacker unit is led by last year’s defensive rookie of the year, Carson Schwesinger, who racked up 156 tackles in 2025 and
leads the team with 35 this year.

With Devin Bush now in Chicago and Jeremiah Owusu-Koramoah still on the PUP list, the other starter is a familiar face, Quincy Williams, who signed for the Browns during the offseason. The main thing that is different about Williams’ role with the Browns is that he’s blitzing at a much higher rate. The Jets have had some issue with blitz pick-ups in key moments, so hopefully that’s something they’ll have been working on all week.

Easton Mascarenas-Arnold is also listed as a starter, but the Browns rarely have more than two linebackers on the field so he’s only played 20 snaps in the first four games.

The backups are Winston Reid and fifth round rookie Justin Jefferson.

Defensive Backs

The Browns’ secondary is led by Pro Bowl cornerback Denzel Ward, and the other starting cornerback is Tyson Campbell, who was acquired via trade last season and ended up with 18 pass breakups.

The primary slot cornerback is Myles Harden, who currently leads the team with three pass breakups. Mekhi Blackmon also made one start this year in a game Campbell missed.

The Browns have two reliable veterans at safety in Ronnie Hickman and Grant Delpit, but they also have second round rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, who has been seeing some playing time in three-safety sets.

Additional secondary depth comes in the shape of cornerbacks Noah Igbinoghene and Toriano Pride Jr. and safeties Daniel Thomas and Donovan McMillan.

Special Teams

The Browns’ placekicker is Andre Szmyt, who only missed three field goals last season and is perfect on all kicks this year, including a 56-yard game winner in the last game.

Their punter is the veteran Corey Bojorquez, who is putting up big numbers so far this season.

In the return game, Corley is listed as the main kickoff returner, although Sanders had the most success so far with a 74-yard runback. Concepcion is the punt returner, with Boston listed as his backup.

You will no doubt recall how first quarter touchdown returns by both Kene Nwangwu and Isaiah Williams sparked the Jets to their win over the Browns last season but many of the players from those units have been replaced.

The primary gunners are Corley and Thomas, and their most productive tacklers in kick coverage include McMillon, Whiteheart and McNeil-Warren.

item.title: Cowboys rookie report: Malachi Lawrence gets his first sack against Tampa Bay
item.description: Malachi Lawrence had a solid moment on Thursday night.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas’ 24–16 loss to Tampa Bay on Thursday night provided very little to celebrate and left Cowboys fans feeling extremely frustrated. However, Malachi Lawrence gave the Cowboys something to build on. The first-round edge defender provided their only sack on a night when the defense struggled to get off the field. Tampa Bay rushed for 241 yards, leaving plenty for the young defenders and veterans to improve on.

But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. 

Caleb Downs

(72 defensive snaps | 4 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended)

Downs had a mixed night. PFF charged him with just one completion for no gain, but also two missed tackles against the run. On a night when Dallas needed its last line of defense to finish plays, those misses mattered. His coverage numbers were encouraging, but his tackling needs to be cleaner, a common theme among all the Cowboys defensive players on Thursday.  

Malachi Lawrence

(27 defensive snaps | 2 tackles | 1 TFL | 1 sack | 0 INT | 1 pass defended | 3 pressures)

Lawrence had a standout week among the rookie class this week. His third-quarter sack pushed Jalon Daniels back 11 yards, and he generated three pressures on just 10 pass-rush snaps which is encouraging. This is a strong return from limited opportunities, and another reason to expand his role. The next step is to sustain that disruption with a bigger workload and see what he can handle going forward. 

Jaishawn Barham

(57 defensive snaps | 7 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 pressures)

Barham supplied some resistance, he was credited with five run stops. He allowed only five yards on two coverage targets, although a crucial missed run tackle blemished his night. His individual production offered encouragement despite the defense’s collective struggles. His seven tackles were the most among the rookies and second-most on the team. 

LT Overton

(23 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 1 pressure)

Overton managed one pressure on eight rushes, but his overall impact was limited. One tackle and no backfield finish made this a quiet outing. The best way to put this is Dallas needs more disruption from its rotational defensive linemen.

item.title: If the Saints win/lose vs. Vikings
item.description: What either result could mean for the black and gold in Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints are looking to pick themselves up off the floor after being routed by the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football. They host the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday in yet another pivotal early-season game for the black and gold. Here’s what either outcome could mean for the Saints.

If the Saints win:

A win would garner a collective sigh of relief among Who Dat Nation and restore some of the belief that this team can still win the division this season.

The Vikings have struggled to find the end zone in their last few games. If the defense can find enough to continue that trend, and the offense can squeeze out enough points against a very impressive Vikings defense, New Orleans will win this matchup.

It’s one that the Saints simply have to have.

If the Saints lose:

One usually wants to avoid such hyperbolic descriptions in early October, but another defeat here could start to spell the beginning of the end of the Saints’ playoff hopes.

With Carolina and Atlanta seemingly trending in the right direction, the division would already begin to feel out of reach. A third consecutive defeat, in three home games, would be beyond gut-punching for Kellen Moore and his team.

Anyone who’s been around this league for a while knows the inherently unpredictable and surprising nature of an NFL season. Writing off this team, especially given the way the quarterback has played, can’t be done at this early stage. New Orleans has been on the wrong end of questionable decisions, faced injuries on both sides of the ball, and could’ve easily been 3-0 after the Raiders game.

But nevertheless, the vibes would be particularly sour, and hopes nearly fully deflated, if the Saints fall to 1-4 this week. Another feature of this league is that it is unforgiving.

Do you think the Saints can get it done on Sunday? How has the opening month of the season affected your outlook for the rest of 2026? Let us know in the comments!

item.title: A frustrating London trip sent confidence spiraling, but Daniels’ return could flip the script quickly - survey results
item.description: A tough London trip sent Commanders fan confidence plunging, but returning starters and home-field advantage loom large in coming games
item.content:encoded:
The emotional whiplash of following the Washington Commanders football team hasn’t relented in the first quarter of the season. Just when the Week 3 gritty home upset win against Seattle appeared to stabilize the ship and reignite optimism, a dreary, injury-filled and mistake-prone Sunday game in London last week against Daniel Jones and the Colts sent fan confidence careening back down the hill.

In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked, as we do every week, about fan confidence, and we looked at the schedule for the coming month to see what fans expect from a critical three-game stretch that includes 2 games before, and one game after, the Week 7 bye. The poll results reflect a fanbase that is feeling thoroughly beaten down by injuries and inconsistent play — though a closer examination of the upcoming schedule suggests things might not be quite as dire as these results imply.

Here is how the Hogs Haven community voted.

Question 1: Are you confident the Commanders are headed in the right direction?

The weekly roller coaster ride continues.

After sitting at 70% in Week 1, confidence peaked at 83% after Week 2. It then dropped like a stone to 20% in Week 3 after the Jayden Daniels injury in the loss at Dallas, but surged back to 76% following the Seattle win. Now, fan confidence has cratered again, dropping 47 points to just 29% in the wake of the loss in London in which third string rookie QB Athan Kaliakmanis was forced to step up to the plate when injuries sidelined both Jayden Daniels and his backup Marcus Mariota.

The volatility in responses and its connection to the results of the latest game played are pretty obvious.

For others, the skepticism runs deeper than a single Sunday result — underlying the lack of confidence is consistent lack of to overarching sideline execution and preparation:

Still, not everyone in the community is ready to throw in the towel on the coaching staff. As commenter SSP pointed out when looking at the bigger picture:

“There was big risk in choosing both a rookie OC and DC, is it any wonder it might take a few games for them to hit their stride? We beat the defending SB champs, are we there? No, but it feels like there is a plan and we aren’t looking for a quick fix that will fade just as quickly… injuries will happen as well, in the end I don’t see how any long time fan can’t be happy with the direction of the team.”

Question 2: What will the Commanders’ record be over their next 3 games?

Visit our partners at FanDuel

When asked to project the upcoming four-week, three-game stretch that includes the bye week — featuring home games against the Giants and Eagles sandwiched around a road trip to San Francisco and the bye — the pessimism carried over directly. A combined 62% of respondents believe Washington will post a losing record (winning one or zero games), with more than a quarter of those fans bracing for a complete 0-3 shutout.

That apprehension seems extreme, but may be understandable given what fans saw in the first four weeks of the season.

Yet, while dropping a road contest against a powerhouse 49ers squad out west is a very reasonable expectation, writing off both home NFC East matchups seems, to me, to ignore several matchup advantages working in Washington’s favor.

The case for 2-1 and home optimism

Weeks 5 & 8

Consider Week 5against the New York Giants. Washington is actually favored by 3.5 points, and for good reason. New York lost starting rookie quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season to injury, forcing them to turn to an erratic Jameis Winston as the starter (with JJ McCarthy waiting in the wings). While New York currently sits at 3-1, all three of their victories came at MetLife Stadium against opponents with a combined record of just 3-6. They have not proven they can win away from home, having lost their only road game of the season. Furthermore, Dan Quinn has owned this divisional rivalry since arriving in Washington, posting a clean 4-0 record against the Giants over the past two seasons. With a Commanders win on Sunday, the Giants would fall to 3-2 while the Commanders climb to 2-3, just a game out of first place in the division.

Even Giants fans don’t buy the hype of the team’s 3-1 start

The return of JD5
Also, the cavalry appears to be coming over the hill for Washington’s roster. The team said Jayden Daniels will to return under center this Sunday after missing time with his elbow injury. The offensive front—which struggled heavily in London with pass protection and opening run lanes—is also tracking to get cornerstone right guard Sam Cosmi back into the starting lineup alongside other potential reinforcements on both sides of the ball.

The evidence of the win over Seattle
Washington is undefeated in its only true home appearance at Northwest Stadium this season, having grinded out that 33-31 win over Seattle – a game in which Seattle never held the lead, and in which the Commanders offense sat on the ball and watched the final two minutes tick down to 00:00 and victory without trying to advance down the field or score. Washington beat Seattle more comprehensively than the scoreboard or box score would indicate.

Looking ahead to Week 8 against Philadelphia, Washington will have the immense advantage of playing at home coming directly off their bye week, giving the coaching staff an extra week of prep and battered players an extra week of recovery.

Meanwhile, Philadelphia has been looking pretty vulnerable through the first month of the season. Under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, the Eagles’ offense has sputtered through disjointed series, and struggled with third-down efficiency. Their once-dominant offensive line took a crushing blow with the sudden, unexpected retirement of All-Pro right tackle Lane Johnson, and the rest of their roster, already depleted with the trade of AJ Brown to New England, has been plagued by a rash of injuries that may be at least as extensive as those that have struck Washington’s roster. In the trenches and along the perimeter, they simply are not the terrifying juggernaut that rolled into the NFC Championship two seasons ago. Fans and media in Philly are once again calling for Nick Sirianni’s head, and this time, I get the sense that they might actually get it.

My expectations for what lies ahead

The next 4 weeks
A 2-1 mark across the upcoming three-game block in October and early November simply does not strike me as wishful thinking; in my mind, it is a very realistic outcome if Washington takes advantage of (finally) enjoying the benefits of playing at home and getting some time to rest and recover in Week 7.

Weeks 9 to 16
There is a compelling argument that Washington can successfully defend its home turf in Weeks 5 and 8 and enter the ninth week of the season just one game below .500 and facing a string of at least 7 winnable games that include the Giants (again), Bengals, Cardinals, Titans, Texans, Falcons, and Vikings. It doesn’t take much imagination to see the Commanders heading to Jacksonville in Week 17 with a winning record and in the hunt for a playoff berth.

It starts this weekend
In any event, the turnaround begins this Sunday, when the Commanders host the New York Giants at Northwest Stadium in Landover.

  • Kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on FOX.
  • Per FanDuel, the Commanders are favored (-3.5) with the over/under set at a very low 43.5 points.

Pack the stands, get loud, and let’s see if the burgundy & gold can take care of business at home.

item.title: What do you think of Matthew Stafford’s start to 2026?
item.description: Matthew Stafford’s start to the season has been high and low, and other NFL news and talking points on a Saturday
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Stafford has thrown 6 interceptions in four games with over 1,100 passing yards (21 rushing yards) and six touchdowns. You can debate how Stafford’s start to the season has been because the six interceptions aren’t ideal, but the other stats are pretty good. So, how you think his start to 2026 has been?

Stafford can still sling it. Below is an attention-grabbing idea of “Father Time catching up with Stafford”, and four games in it doesn’t quite look like that.

It does look like Stafford may not match his MVP level of play in 2025.

Then again, you could argue if Stafford can cut the picks, keep up and or increase the production, then he could regain that type of MVP form. The odds of Stafford winning back-to-back MVP’s are incredibly unlikely so we aren’t saying that. Still, so far, he has shown the arm to deliver that type of high caliber performances and moments.

It’s been a bit of a polarizing start to the season for Stafford and the Rams, and with a 2-2 record, polarizing making plenty of sense as the description of the team to this point.

They play their best at times; they play their worst at times. They’re polarizing. Stafford’s play has been a part of that.

‘Has Father Time Caught Up With You?’ — NFL Analyst Puts Matthew Stafford on Notice After Reigning MVP’s Worrying Start To Season (sports.yahoo)

“Chris Broussard Questions Whether Matthew Stafford Is Showing His Age

During “First Things First,” Broussard challenged Stafford to show that his best football remains available on a consistent basis.

“Matthew Stafford, has father time caught up with you? I think that’s a legitimate question at this point,”Broussard said.

He acknowledged that Stafford still delivers impressive moments. His concern was how much those flashes actually reveal about the quarterback’s overall level of play.

“At times, you still look great, but that’s what happens. Even old guys can look great at times,” Broussard continued.

Broussard pointed to Stafford’s six interceptions through four games, including four over his previous two appearances. He then delivered the challenge behind his assessment.

“So, you have to go out there and prove that you are still that guy,”Broussard said.“

Matthew Stafford evaluates his performance in Rams’ first 4 games (ramswire)

Matthew Stafford took home his first MVP award last season after throwing for a league-high 4,707 yards and 46 touchdowns. His numbers to start this year have paled in comparison, only tossing six touchdown passes and six interceptions in four games.

Suffice to say, it’s been an up-and-down season thus far, mixing big-time throws with costly mistakes that have led to turnovers and points for the other team.

Now that the first quarter of the season is in the books, Stafford evaluated his play when asked during Thursday’s press conference. He admitted he can certainly be better and wishes he had some throws back.

“Definitely room for improvement,” he said. “There have been some really bright moments and some stuff I’m really proud of and stuff that I definitely wish I could take back to help us be in a better position to win games. That comes with the position. I understand that. I’ve been doing it a long time. I want to do everything I can to put our team in the best position to succeed. I’ve done that sometimes this year and other times I have not. I want to make sure that I do that at a more consistent clip moving forward.”

Matthew Stafford Isn’t Hiding From His Turnovers, and the Rams Need It to Show Against Buffalo (athlonsports)

“The Rams are 2-2 with an offense that ranks second in total yards and 19th in scoring. Eight giveaways have a lot to do with that gap. PFF has charged Stafford with eight turnover-worthy plays, which ranks 28th among quarterbacks, and his 65.4 grade sits 22nd of 34. Sumer Sports lists the Rams with the league’s fourth-highest interception rate at 3.64%. He threw a pick-six in Denver during a 30-26 loss, then two more interceptions in the first half against the Eagles before the 24-20 comeback.“

Fantasy football Week 5 Start ‘Em & Sit ‘Em: Matthew Stafford gets right back on track vs. Bills (cbssports)

“It’s been a rocky start to the season so far for Stafford, but he should have a dominant game in Week 5 against Buffalo. I like Stafford as a top-three Fantasy quarterback in all leagues. He has two games this year with at least 24.9 Fantasy points and two others with 9.7 Fantasy points or less. Puka Nacua missed two games with a groin injury, but he’s healthy now. And Stafford is throwing the ball a lot with at least 51 pass attempts in his past two outings against Denver and Philadelphia. He’s only played one game at home this season (Week 2 against the Giants), and Stafford scored 34.9 Fantasy points. This week, we could get a shootout against the Bills, who are No. 5 in most Fantasy points allowed to opposing quarterbacks. C.J. Stroud, Jared Goff and Drake Maye each scored at least 20.5 Fantasy points against Buffalo, with Goff and Maye going over 32 Fantasy points. That’s the expectation I have for Stafford, who should be in a potential shootout with Josh Allen since this game has a projected total score of 53.5 points. I’m excited to see how good Stafford can be in Week 5, and he should have one of his best games of the season against Buffalo at home.”

All eyes on SoFi Stadium as the Rams & the Bills battle on MNF | Game Preview (therams.com)

“If you love tight end play, this is the game for you. According to NFL Pro, the Bills have used multiple tight ends on more than half their plays this season, buying into the Rams-led league-wide trend. However, with Colby Parkinson and Terrance Ferguson injured last week, the Rams used 13 personnel on just one snap, their fewest in a full calendar year. Fortunately, Parkinson is trending in the right direction to return, and it doesn’t sound like Ferguson should miss more than the required four weeks on injured reserve. In the meantime, Tyler Higbee has found the fountain of youth.
