item.title: 2026 Fantasy Football Rookie Report: Denzel Boston emerges, Carnell Tate surges
item.description: Aditya Fuldeore breaks down 2026 NFL rookies' key trends and fantasy outlook every quarter of the season. Denzel Boston has surged to the top of the rookie rankings while Carnell Tate picks up his production and Jeremiyah Love deals with ankle injuries.
item.content:encoded:
Another new season is here to bring in a new rookie class with a lot of fantasy football uncertainty. Despite the injection of new talent, rookie usage and trends may not have fantasy managers jumping for joy just yet. Here, I aim to give you an update every quarter of the NFL season on how rookies are doing and their fantasy values. As we approach Week 5, trends are beginning to form for top rookies.

Rookie rankings

Top 10 fantasy rookies to roster right now

1. RB Jeremiyah Love, ARI
2. WR Denzel Boston, CLE
3. WR Carnell Tate, TEN
4. TE Kenyon Sadiq, NYJ
5. WR KC Concepcion, CLE
6. WR Antonio Williams, WAS
7. WR Jordyn Tyson, NO
8. WR Ted Hurst, TB
9. WR Malachi Fields, NYG
10. WR Makai Lemon, PHI

Just four games into the season, injuries and slow starts shake the rookie leaderboard out with some unexpected contributors. We’ll see some injured players (Jordyn Tyson) soon, and maybe even some quarterbacks (Fernando Mendoza). Between no immediate starting quarterbacks and a banged-up running back (Jadarian Price, Jonah Coleman) class, it’s the wide receiver position having the most fantasy viability of the 2026 group.

Biggest risers and fallers since start of season

Risers

Cleveland Browns WR Denzel Boston

Boston was drafted as the second Browns rookie off the board with an ADP around WR60, well beyond the top-120 draft picks. He is now the leading rookie receivers in fantasy points per game, catching 13-of-23 targets for 286 yards and two touchdowns on the season. The Browns have utilized Boston as the team’s deep-ball receiver and his 18.0 average depth of target is No. 5 among all receivers. Boston is squarely in the fantasy WR3 range as a result.

60 YARDS DOWN THE FIELD FOR DB!#PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrimepic.twitter.com/9rrJl5NINH

— Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026

New York Jets TE Kenyon Sadiq

Though he was already drafted in the mid-to-low end fantasy TE2 range before the season, Sadiq is a riser after the first quarter of the NFL season. He has caught 12-of-18 targets for 143 yards and a touchdown through the air, scoring his first career touchdown with a three-yard carry in Week 1. The Jets made it a point to get him designed touches early and he exploded with 105 yards in Week 3. though he laid an egg in Week 4, it was a historically low-volume game for the Jets. Sadiq is a high-end TE2 moving forward.

Fallers

Seattle Seahawks RB Jadarian Price

Price was the second Notre Dame running back off the board in the first round, heading to a Seahawks team that lost Kenneth Walker and had Zach Charbonnet start the season recovering from a torn ACL. He debuted playing 48-percent of the Seahawks’ offensive snaps in Week 1, leading a committee backfield. Fumbles in back-to-back weeks dented Price’s production before a chest injury put him on injured reserve. Price was taken around RB25 this season but is an IR stash with RB4 viability later in the season.

Philadelphia Eagles WR Makai Lemon

Results and expectations not aligning is the main driver of a fantasy value dip. So, we have another first-rounder; Lemon’s unusable is a byproduct of the disappointing Eagles offense. He’s seen several touches behind the line of scrimmage, averaging 6.5 yards per reception. A total of 15 targets has yielded 65 scoreless receiving with negative five rushing yards. Devonta Smith’s hamstring injury may give Lemon more opportunities, but the Eagles offensive environment is hostile to fantasy production. He is a dart-throw for fantasy points at this stage of the season.

▶ Position-by-position report

Quarterbacks

The 2026 quarterback class has not yielded any weekly starters yet. No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza currently sits behind veteran Kirk Cousins for a surprising upstart Raiders team. A 3-1 start keeps Cousins in the starting spot for longer, but Mendoza is still a possibility to make an appearance the second half of the season.

The two quarterbacks that have debuted are seventh-round pick Athan Kaliakmanis and undrafted free agent Jalon Daniels. The Commanders’ first two quarterbacks were hurt in Week 4, prompting Kaliakmanis to enter the game and make some splash throws in the team’s loss to the Colts. Daniels is the Buccaneers starter with Baker Mayfield out; he started Week 4 and will be a fantasy QB3 until Mayfield’s return.

Athan Kaliakmanis goes DEEP for a beauty of a touchdown!@INDvsWAS on NFL Network
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/JXB6CmxI9w

— NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026

Running Backs

The running back class for 2026 starts with a pair of Notre Dame running backs and sprinkles into a few quality backup runners. The chart below shows that Jeremiyah Love is the only running back thus far with some sort of starting opportunity. As a result, he is the only running back fantasy managers will consider starting on a weekly basis, though ankle issues may throw a wrench in some of his opportunities.

Wide Receivers

The 2026 rookie class has yet to have an alpha every-week starter emerge, but there are a few with the paths to head there. The chart below shows Carnell Tate and the Browns rookie duo getting the most targets en route to fantasy production. Despite lower opportunities, JoshCameron is efficiently getting fantasy value out of little opportunities.

Tight Ends

The only fantasy-relevant rookie tight end thus far has been Kenyon Sadiq. Though Mason Taylor (thumb) will return to the tight end rotation soon, Adonai Mitchell and fellow rookie Omar Cooper are still dealing with injuries. I touched on him having rising value earlier in this column; Sadiq is worth rostering beyond just streamer tight end value.

Matthew Hibner and Eli Raridon have also seen small volume as a part of their offenses. Hibner has five receptions for 70 yards and a touchdown with the Ravens. Raridon has caught three passes for 44 yards and a touchdown with the Pats. They are worth rostering in Dynasty leagues as the potential futures of their respective tight end rooms.

▶ Looking ahead

Rookies whose roles could change before the next quarterly rookie report.

Miami Dolphins WR Chris Bell

For standard 12-team leagues, it’s time to think of streamers and stashes as bye weeks approach. Bell is coming off a torn ACL and has seen increased snaps while the Dolphins’ other third-round receiver, Caleb Douglas, nurses an ankle injury. He had a 68-yard touchdown wiped out by a toenail in Week 4 and has a good chance to earn and keep a larger role in an unproven Dolphins receiving corps.

Chris Bell showing off his speed @KCvsMIA on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/tNbGIYPEGf

— NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026

Jacksonville Jaguars WR Josh Cameron

The Jaguars have a very fantasy friendly offense, with Cameron having a role in 12 personnel. Liam Coen has given the sixth-round rookie a role garnering around a third of the team’s offensive snaps. He’s caught two touchdowns and would see a bump in usage if Brian Thomas Jr. is traded away this season. Cameron is a candidate to see a role increase over the next quarter of the season as a player already making an impact and having his target competition on the trade block.

New Orleans Saints RB CJ Donaldson

Let’s dig deeper through the grit and grime and really look for a deep league target…Undrafted rookie CJ Donaldson finds himself on this list just four weeks into the season as a result of the Saints’ ambiguous backfield. Travis Etienne is on injured reserve, Kendre Miller has been ineffective, and Alvin Kamara is 31 years-old with his own injury history. It see a larger role over the next quarter of the season.

Various stats from Pro Football Reference and PFF.

item.title: Jeremiah Trotter Jr. has earned his chance to start
item.description: Philadelphia’s backup linebacker deserves more playing time.
item.content:encoded:
At the time a few years ago, Jeremiah Trotter Jr. was considered a “pity pick” by some in the Eagles’ organization, when he was taken with the second of the Eagles’ three fifth-round picks in the 2024 NFL Draft at No. 155 overall.

Trotter Jr. has since proven in these last two seasons that he is more than that.

If anyone bared to notice last Sunday in the Eagles’ nightmare 24-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, the No. 2 offense in the NFL averaging 417 yards and No. 2 averaging 290.3 yards a game, Trotter had a game-high 15 tackles, 10 solo. In part-time duty, he’s No. 6 overall on the Eagles in tackles with 19 tackles, tied with starting cornerback Quinyon Mitchell and one behind starting safety Andrew Mukuba.

Playing in place of the injured Zack Baun, Trotter was all over the field. The 15 tackles were a season-high performance for any Eagles defender so far this year. The performance also came after Trotter led the Eagles in tackles during preseason.

Eagles’ defensive coordinator Vic Fangio certainly noticed Trotter against the Rams.

When asked how Trotter played against Los Angeles, and if that merited more playing time, Fangio said, “Yeah, he played very well. Did a good job … Possibly, yeah (more playing time).”

Trotter has the support of many in the Jefferson Health Training Complex, especially Fangio. What Fangio may be facing is the fact Eagles’ general manager selected Jihaad Campbell in the first round of the 2025 NFL Draft (31st pick overall). Being a first-round selection comes with the immediate pressure to perform, which Campbell has done sporadically, though not consistently. Campbell, listed at 6-foot-3, 235 pounds, may be better served as an edge rusher with the ball in front of him, instead of working in space, where he tends to lose receivers.

A classic example of that came in the season opener against Washington. Campbell completely lost Commanders’ rookie Antonio Williams for a 33-yard reception on a third-and-14 play at the Eagles’ 47 with 12:12 left to play. It led to a Washington touchdown with 9:59 to play. How Campbell lost Williams was baffling.

The Eagles have some thinking to do. Trotter’s contract is up in 2028. The Eagles can extend Trotter after the 2027 season. Roseman drafted Campbell with the intention of contributing as an edge rusher, and he did bear up well for a time before Fangio thought Campbell was better at linebacker. Against the Chicago Bears, a couple of them who were on the field against Campbell, they admitted Campbell was a great athlete with a great future ahead of him though was also someone right now who “doesn’t know what he’s doing.”    

Campbell leads the Eagles with 37 tackles, but he is still learning at a slow pace. Plus, as a Roseman first-round pick, that carries some weight, regardless of how lost he sometimes looks in coverage.

Trotter will continue to do what he does, keeps his head down, immerses himself in game film, and never stirs drama. He’s about football. He’s always been about football, since he starred at St Joe’s Prep, and Clemson, and now, it seems, casting a larger role with the Eagles. He once played under the large shadow of his dad, “as the son of former Eagles’ great Jeremiah Trotter Sr.” It is a shadow long since faded. The only thing missing for Jeremiah Trotter Jr. now is opportunity, because he has certainly proved he can start in the NFL—and for the Eagles.

item.title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 6 of NCAA Football Season
item.description: Here are three prospects Broncos Country should watch for in Week 6 of the NCAA Football season.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to another installment of Future Broncos. Based on the comments section, a lot of you are wanting the scoop and information on offensive linemen and inside linebackers. I’ll dedicate a spot each to those position groups for Week 6 of the college football season. Here are three prospects to watch.

Elijah Paige — Left Tackle — USC

With Garett Bolles and Mike McGlinchey getting up there in age, there is good reason fans across Broncos Country want the franchise to invest in the tackle position in the 2027 NFL Draft. There hasn’t been a premium draft day investment there in a decade. Truth be told, Denver’s offensive line certainly could use some long-term additions at multiple spots. They haven’t been playing as well as they have the past two seasons.

One player to watch as the collegiate season continues is USC redshirt junior left tackle Elijah Paige. Paige didn’t play much during his freshman season. However, he started thirteen games for the Trojans at left tackle in 2024. Injuries plagued his 2025 campaign and limited the blindside protector to just seven starts at left tackle. However, was credited with just six quarterback pressures and no sacks last season.

Paige (6’7” and 315 pounds) is regarded as one of the top pass protectors in this year’s draft. He’s got prototypical size and length for the position. I believe #72 is big reason why quarterback Jayden Maiava is playing at a high level this year. However, I do have some concerns. His strength at the point of the attack and technique in the run game needs a lot of work. His athleticism and movement skills stick out in zone runs, but there is certainly room for improvement with gap principles in Lincoln Riley’s offense.

The traits and tools are there. If he can stay healthy and continue to get better in the aforementioned areas, he definitely has first-round potential. You can catch Page in action this evening when the #19 ranked Trojans take on Penn State.

Kam Robinson — Inside Linebacker — Virginia

Thus far, I’ve covered Georgia’s standout Chris Cole and ultra-productive Texas Tech star Ben Roberts at inside linebacker. Those two will be high draft picks next April. Several other linebackers in this class are thought highly of, but Virginia standout Kam Robinson is a prospect who is significantly underrated.

Last season, Robinson was dominant. In eight games, he posted 64 tackles, 4.5 tackles for loss, a safety, as well as 2 interceptions—both of which were returned for touchdowns. He was undoubtedly Virginia’s best defensive player and is a true three-down linebacker at the next level. Unfortunately, he tore his ACL in November against Duke and missed the rest of his junior season.

This year, Robinson (6’2”, 239 pounds) is looking to showcase his talents again with a rebound campaign. Even though he has over three hundred career tackles, he is determined to prove to general managers and scouts he can be a long-term starter in the NFL. He missed the season opener recovering from the ACL injury and has eighteen tackles in four games thus far.

He’s one of the most well-rounded linebackers in the country. He does a great job on blitzes getting pressure on the quarterback. He sports the athleticism and range to play sideline-to-sideline, but also shows a good knack for moving downhill, shedding blocks, and making plays near the line of scrimmage. Robinson has been a key cog in the Cavaliers’ special team’s units as well.

Where Robinson ultimately gets drafted will depend on how his medicals check out and his performance the rest of the season. As of now, I’d peg him as a Top 100 pick with a chance to rise significantly if things go well moving forward. You can catch Robinson in action tonight in an ACC matchup when they host Syracuse.

Jelani McDonald — Defensive Back — Texas

Defensive back isn’t a top-tier need for the Broncos just yet. However, it’s important to remind folks cornerbacks Riley Moss and Ja’Quan McMillian are slated to hit free agency, as well as safety Brandon Jones. Second-year player Jahdae Barron will certainly wind up replacing one of the corners. However, adding a defensive back for the long haul seems like a possibility for Denver with their large slate of draft picks.

One of the top defensive backs in this year’s class is Texas standout Jelani McDonald. In a loaded Longhorns secondary, McDonald didn’t make an impact in his freshman season back in 2023 on defense. Though he was a stalwart on their special team’s unit. Since then, McDonald been a key player for Steve Sarkisian’s squad and is considered one of the best defensive backs in the nation.

McDonald (6’2”, 200 pounds) is coming off a junior campaign where he posted 80 tackles, 3 interceptions, and 1 fumble recovery. In four games thus far, McDonald has 26 tackles and has logged a lot of snaps in the Longhorns’ secondary. He is considered one of their defensive leaders and is routinely praised by the coaching staff for his football intelligence, work ethic, and passion for the game.

Like is former teammate Barron, McDonald has played just about everywhere for the Longhorns. He rarely comes off the field and always appears to be in a position to make a play on the ball. I love his ferocious nature up in the box defending against the run. He lays the wood with his tackling. I’ve also come away equally impressed with the senior’s coverage ability from split-zone looks, inside at nickel, to even his smaller sample size in single-high looks.

He’s just a great prospect that can do it all. While I don’t envision defensive back being a Top 50 consideration for Denver at this juncture, McDonald is a prospect whose prowess in multiple phases and versatility merits early consideration in the ‘27 NFL Draft. Y0u can catch McDonald in action this afternoon when the top-ranked Longhorns take on the Oklahoma Sooners.

item.title: Chicago Bears Week 5 Flashbacks: Sweetness hits 100, an NFL Record is set, and a win in Lambeau
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 5 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
1.) 1985, Bears @ Buccaneers: Walter Payton reaches 100 touchdowns

October 6, 1985 | Bears win 27-19

The eventual Super Bowl champions entered Tampa Bay undefeated, but the winless Buccaneers weren’t particularly interested in rolling over.

Chicago trailed 12-3 at halftime before Jim McMahon helped engineer a second-half comeback, completing 14 of 17 passes after intermission.

The biggest story, however, belonged to Walter Payton.

Payton scored on a four-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter, becoming just the sixth player in NFL history to reach 100 career touchdowns. He added his 101st on a nine-yard run with 52 seconds remaining, sealing Chicago’s 27-19 victory.

McMahon finished with 292 passing yards, while Payton recorded 63 rushing yards and two touchdowns. The defense also held Tampa Bay running back James Wilder to just 29 yards on 18 carries.

The victory moved Chicago to 5-0, its best start since the 1963 championship season.

2.) 2012, Bears @ Jaguars: Peanut and Briggs make NFL history

October 7, 2012 | Bears win 41-3

The 2012 Bears defense had developed a rather enjoyable habit of turning opposing quarterbacks’ mistakes into points.

That trend continued in Jacksonville.

After entering halftime tied 3-3, Chicago exploded for 38 unanswered points in the second half, highlighted by a pair of defensive touchdowns.

Charles Tillman intercepted Blaine Gabbert and returned it 36 yards for a touchdown in the third quarter. Lance Briggs followed with a 36-yard interception return of his own in the fourth.

The two became the first teammates in NFL history to return interceptions for touchdowns in consecutive games, having accomplished the same feat against Dallas six days earlier.

Tillman’s touchdown was also the eighth defensive score of his career, establishing a new Bears franchise record.

The offense eventually joined the fun, with Jay Cutler throwing for 292 yards and two touchdowns, Brandon Marshall catching 12 passes for 144 yards, and Matt Forte rushing for 107 yards.

Chicago improved to 4-1 heading into its bye week.

3.) 2000, Bears @ Packers: Chicago finally breaks through

The 2000 season had not exactly gotten off to the start Chicago was hoping for.

The Bears entered Week 5 at 0-4 before heading north to Lambeau Field, where Brett Favre and the Packers were waiting.

Naturally, that is where everything finally clicked.

Cade McNown opened the scoring with a one-yard touchdown run before connecting with Marcus Robinson for touchdown passes of 68 and 58 yards. Robinson somehow turned just two catches into 126 yards and two touchdowns as Chicago built a 24-3 lead midway through the third quarter.

Green Bay eventually made things interesting.

Favre threw three second-half touchdown passes as the Packers cut the deficit to three, but Paul Edinger’s 47-yard field goal with just over three minutes remaining gave Chicago enough breathing room to hold on for a 27-24 victory.

McNown finished 11-of-20 for 203 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions, while adding 51 yards and another score on the ground.

Maybe most importantly, the Bears did not turn the football over once while forcing three Green Bay giveaways.

The victory gave Chicago its first win of the season, and doing it at Lambeau Field certainly made an otherwise rough start a little easier to swallow.

If you are going to finally get into the win column, beating the Packers is a pretty good way to do it.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: Roster help, Tae Banks, J.J. McCarthy, Bryan Hudson, more
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions, answers about the first-place Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Wayne Wright asks: Any idea why there was no extra point try after the Banks touchdown at the end of the Cardinals game? Obviously the point wasn’t needed, but it seems to me that we always see extra point attempts in similar situations in other games. Although it’s not likely to matter, I do know that points scored is one of the tie-breakers for who gets a playoff spot at the end of the season. Do you have any info on this? 

Ed says: Wayne, the league changed the rule in 2018. An extra point at the end of a game that does not impact the outcome is no longer required. If you look at the tiebreakers, the point total is so far down the list that it is really deemed inconsequential.

Dumpster Dan asks: I know that the Giants always look to see if they can improve the roster and it was generally thought that they were looking for DL and CB help. Do you think the 3-1 start has changed anything? Does the loss of Burns increase their looking for DL help?

Ed says: Dan, I really don’t believe it changes much. They will try to help the roster if they can, but they have to keep in mind that they can’t give away a lot of resources for short-term fixes. If you can get young players you think are difference-makers you have a chance to keep for a few years, that’s different.

I do think the wide-open nature of the NFC East increases the temptation to make a move or two to improve the team’s opportunity this season.

Martin Hand asks: Ed, since Banks has been playing so well, what is your prediction on his contract status?

Ed says: Martin, that’s an interesting one. Before the season, I would have said the idea of an extension for Banks would have been laughable. Now? If he continues to play well, and continues to show an improved attitude, I could see an extension of a couple of years being where things land.

The projected franchise tag, per Over The Cap, is $23.119 million for cornerbacks. I can’t see that, but I can certainly see an extension. There are 13 games to go, though, so we will see where it lands.

DWopper2 asks: All during camp there was so much talk about Patrick Ricard blasting open holes for the running backs. In the Dallas game that worked very well, and he seemed to be a real weapon for the offense. Where has he been since? Against the Cardinals, there were plays where he went into the line on the other side of center from where the running backs went. How does that help? I did not go back to watch the game again, but wondering if he had any impact on the game whatsoever. If he is not a blocking machine, would it be better to have both Skat and Tracy (or Harris) in the backfield so the defense does not know who might get the ball and what direction they will go?

Ed says: Wopper, the days of two running backs in a T formation where you weren’t always sure which one was getting the ball are long gone. Teams play with a runner and a lead blocker. Only on rare occasions does any team use a two-back set with two true running backs.

As for your Patrick Ricard question, I think the struggles with the running game are not Ricard-related. They are more about the absence of Jaxson Dart.

Dart ran 11 times for 54 yards (4.9 yards per carry) in the season opener. His 22-yard run in that game is the longest the Giants have this season. No running back has a carry of longer than 13 yards.

The Giants’ offense was built with Dart’s ability to run being a major part of the playbook, and a major way they would try to create explosive plays. Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris are power runners who are rarely going to make guys miss at the second level and have those long runs.

Tyrone Tracy is the closest thing they have to a big-play back. They might have to give him more opportunities. More options and efficiency in the run game is also part of why we are probably going to see some of J.J. McCarthy at times. He is not the dangerous runner that Dart is, but he does give the Giants the opportunity to use pieces of the playbook that Jameis Winston does not.

Norm Weiss asks: Ed, I read Nick Falato’s article about whether Bryan Hudson or John Michael Schmitz should start, after which the fan survey had 71% in favor of Hudson. Although Schmitz has not lived up to expectations, he has been an average solid center. I can’t help but feel that if Schmitz was the UFA & Hudson was the 2nd round pick that survey results would look quite different. Also, as Nick pointed out the interior defensive line of the Cardinals isn’t anywhere near as good as the defensive tackles on Dallas, LA or Tennessee. We still didn’t get much of a push from our interior offensive line or open up many holes in the run game against Arizona. I’d love to hear your thoughts on Hudson vs. Schmitz and why we haven’t generated much push from our interior offensive line since the Cowboy game.

Ed says: Norm, I explained why I think Hudson should be the starter here. In short, it comes down to this. I think the Giants will move on from Schmitz after this season. Hudson looks as though he might be capable. I feel like the Giants should give him enough run to find out one way or the other.

Taj Siddiqi asks: With Jameis Winston at QB we are winning dangerously. He is not the future even with his current contract. What is the harm in inserting JJ McCarthy as our starting quarterback in next couple of weeks just to find out if he could be our number one or at least a competent number two.

Ed says: Taj, everyone understands Jaxson Dart is the future at quarterback. There will be week-to-week conjecture in the media and fan base about when, or if, McCarthy should replace Winston.

First, let me ask a question. McCarthy has played 10 games. A team without good quarterback, and with a head coach considered to be a great quarterbacks coach, had him as third-string behind Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz. They couldn’t wait to get rid of him, dumping him before the season was even one-fourth over. Why are so many people convinced that McCarthy will be better than Winston, and that playing him is a good idea? Maybe it will work, but it did not in Minnesota. Playing him in New York could easily be a disaster.

Another factor is that you can’t start McCarthy until he knows enough of the offense, and has worked enough with new teammates, to be comfortable. Can you send him out there and expect him to play winning football if he knows maybe 30% of the playbook and hasn’t really had an opportunity to practice with Malik Nabers, Isaiah Likely, and Darnell Mooney?

Finally, there is this. Jameis Winston is a highly-respected player in the Giants’ locker room. He is a team captain and part of the team’s player Leadership Council. Those things are rarely bestowed upon a guy who starts the season as the backup quarterbacker. Winston has a lot of support on that team. The Giants need to be very careful about not creating a situation that splits the locker room. If the Giants turn to McCarthy, you can guarantee there will be players wondering what the kid did to deserve taking Winston’s spot. Quarterback controversies oftenend up doing that, and it will be interesting to see how John Harbaugh navigates trying to avoid that.

Joel Friedberg asks: Since one of (Jaxson) Dart’s main strengths was running with the football and since it is also a strength of McCarthy what do you think of the idea of putting in a short yardage zone read package for McCarthy where he could hand off or run a nd even pull it once in a while and pass. Maybe 1 or 2 plays that he could run and get good at?

Ed says: Joel, the Giants did have a McCarthy package ready against the Arizona Cardinals. They will have one against the Washington Commanders, as well. It makes sense because McCarthy is younger and more mobile than Jameis Winston. The difficulty with that is not becoming predictable when and if you put McCarthy on the field.

Michael Spina asks: As I understand, there is no cap relief when a player is lost for the season. It seems to me (and please correct me if I’m wrong) that severe and season-ending injuries are more prevalent in the modern game. Do you know if the NFL is considering or has ever considered a form of cap relief when a player is lost to injury?

Ed says: Michael, the NFL has a hard cap. Players assume the risk of getting hurt by playing the sport. Teams assume the risk with every player they sign. This is why teams always talk about leaving themselves room under the cap for the inevitable injuries that will cause them to add players.

Do you really want to “reward” a team that loses a star player by giving them cap relief that lets them go out and acquire another star player?

Here is a look at how the Giants fared last season in relation to the rest of the league in cap money lost to players on injured reserve.

John Foti asks: Defenses have become very adept at causing fumbles by punching the ball out of the ball carriers’ grasp. Sometimes it’s just a great play by the defender. The ball carrier has the ball tightly tucked away and somehow it gets punched out. Other times though, especially when we see gang tackling, a defender stands up the ball carrier or holds the ball carriers’ free arm as other defenders try to pull the ball out. I have never felt that was fair and  feel that it should not be legal. What’s your thought on that?

Ed says: John, I don’t like it. I think referees are sometimes way too slow to blow a play dead when it turns into a scrum. The “peanut punch”, though, is a real thing. Jevon Holland happens to be good at it.

Matt Totaro asks: Hey Ed, with all the season ending injuries this year for the Giants, looking back at past seasons ruined by injuries, who’s your ultimate what if? Outside of the self inflicted gunshot one.

Ed says: Matt, when it comes to injury-related “what-if’s” I really don’t have one. I will give you and our readers a couple to chew on, though:

  • What if the Giants had moved on from GM Jerry Reese and quarterback Eli Manning in 2015 when they let Tom Coughlin go? That is what I have always said I thought they should have done. Start fresh.
  • What if Justin Herbert had declared for the 2019 NFL Draft? I think Dave Gettleman would have moved heaven and earth to make sure the Giants were able to select him.

Francis Castros asks: What do you know about JDart’s current status? Is he rehabbing daily at the Quest Diagnostics Training Center? Is he in communication with J.J. McCarthy? Will he be attending games?

Ed says: Francis, we don’t see Jaxson Dart or get to talk to him. We probably won’t officially talk to him until the end of the season. I have to believe he will attend meetings, be around, and rehab at the facility as much as he can. As for attending games, that becomes a matter of whether he is physically able and whether it is safe for him to do so.

I wasn’t there on Friday, but there was word that Dart was seen around the facility by media for the first time since his surgery.

Michael Spezio asks: Ed, what are you and the BBV staff hearing about J.J. McCarthy now that he’s had a couple of weeks in the building? Beyond the public praise, how far along is he in Matt Nagy’s offense, and is he getting any first-team reps yet, or still mostly scout team?

If he’s called on, do you think he can show the same quick uptake Dart did, or that Jalon Daniels just did in Tampa? Or is that “quick success” thinner than it looks? Dart’s 2026 is basically one game, Daniels has two starts, and both of their good games came against a Dallas defense that keeps giving up points.

Ed says: Michael, what we have been told — and the tiny bit I have seen at practice — is what we know. You have to realize that McCarthy has been a Giant for just a little more than a week. The Giants have been practicing since April. There is no way he knows the full playbook yet, or close to it.

Jaxson Dart took every first-team rep from April until he got injured. As for first-team reps now, those are going to Jameis Winston. He needs them to be as ready to play as he can be — he didn’t get them in the spring and summer.

As for Jalon Daniels, again, you have to understand he has been with the Bucs since April. He played surprisingly well Thursday night, but that amount of time is a huge help.

I don’t understand this rush the fan base seems to be in to get McCarthy into the lineup. I know Jameis Winston is an adventure, and him being the starter isn’t ideal. What evidence, though, is there that McCarthy can be a good quarterback? The Vikings drafted him 10th overall, and the last thing they wanted to do is actually play him. He was No. 3 behind Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz, neither of whom is really all that good. The Vikings couldn’t wait to get rid of him.

You might see McCarthy starting at some point. I just don’t get why everyone is in such a hurry.

Doug Mollin asks: In your “5 questions” piece, the Commanders writer recommended:

“To attack the offense, I would use a QB spy to limit Jayden’s rushing and only rush four, dropping the rest back in coverage. Jayden has been very good at reading the blitz and throwing quickly or using his legs to avoid it, so dropping more back in coverage and shifting coverages has generally been more effective at preventing him from making a play.”

I get the logic of that statement, but boy was it fun watching our defense play the last 3 quarters against Arizona.

How much does a DC/HC tailor the defensive game plan to that opponent versus forcing their will on the opponent?

Do you think we’ll run that Arizona style defense out there again? Or game plan this to contain Jayden?

Ed says: Doug, every team has a base package or a basic style of defense (or offense) that it wants to play. But, within that there are a lot of options and variables.

You can’t run the same defense against a team led by Jayden Daniels and Terry McLaurin that you ran against a team led by Jacoby Brissett and Jeremiyah Love. Brissett is a stationary quarterback, and blitzing him heavily made sense. Blitz Daniels, play man coverage behind it, and he will run for a zillion yards if you don’t sack him every time.

You have to be able to show quarterbacks different looks. You have to be able to use players in a variety of ways. Every opponent is different, and you have to do the best you can within your style to match their strengths.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

item.title: Week 5 Preview: Offensive Breakthrough?
item.description: Will This Finally Be the Week?
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikings are on the road this week to face the New Orleans Saints, a team I projected to win the NFC South but that has sputtered out of the gate at 1-3. The division rival Atlanta Falcons drubbed them 45-24 at home on Monday night. It was their second straight loss at the Superdome.

Can the Vikings make it three in a row? Let’s dive in.

VIKINGS ON OFFENSE

The Vikings’ offense finally lived up to preseason expectations in the 4th quarter of Sunday’s win over the Miami Dolphins. Kevin O’Connell clearly sought to maximize Kyler Murray’s comfort, resulting in the most shotgun formations in any game of his tenure as head coach. Murray responded with an incredibly effective 4th quarter, going 13 of 14 for 120 yards and a 102.4 passer rating. All eyes will be on whether this becomes the new norm or simply an anomaly.

The schedule has worked in our favor as the Vikings’ offense finally finds a rhythm. While the Dolphins’ defense ranked near the bottom in many defensive categories, the Saints’ defense may be worse. They’re dead last in points allowed per game (32.0), 30th in rush yards allowed (147.8), and 26th in both net yards per game (360.3) and yards per play (5.8). If there’s one positive, they’re in the middle of the pack (15th) in passing yards allowed per game (212.5).

KOC and the Saints’ defensive coordinator, Brandon Staley, know each other because they both served on Sean McVay’s staff in L.A., but that works both ways. As the Chargers’ head coach, Staley got the better of KOC in their only matchup since 2022: a 28-24 Chargers win in 2023. But the Vikings moved the ball up and down the field for 475 net yards, with Justin Jefferson catching 7 passes for 149 yards. If memory serves, this was the game when the Chargers took the lead late on a Justin Herbert touchdown pass that bounced off a Vikings cornerback’s helmet. I think that’s the one. Seems about right.

Oh, and there’s the little detail about Odell Beckham, Jr., signing with the Vikings this week. Didn’t see that coming. I don’t expect him to impact Sunday’s game much, if at all, but it’ll be interesting to see what this means heading into the bye. It could simply be an added-depth move given Jefferson’s injury and Jauan Jennings’s failure to make an impact on offense…or…it could mean Jordan Addison is on the trade block. Ehh. Social media rumors and gossip abound. I hope we find out soon.

It’s approaching mid-October. Justin Jefferson should be back and pumped to play in his hometown. You hate to say it’s now or never, but at some point this offense needs a 35-point outburst to calm the nerves and offer some optimism for a tougher stretch ahead. And no, I’m not talking about the Packers fumbling and bumbling the ball away to us on short fields and gifting us drive-saving penalties. I mean long, sustained possessions with chunk plays in the passing game. I know the left side of the offensive line is banged up, but Ryan Van Demark and Joe Huber held their own against the Dolphins. And it won’t be like they’ll be going up against Myles Garrett, T.J. Watt, Chris Jones, or… Dallas Turner! Yeah, I said it.

VIKINGS ON DEFENSE

This is the most interesting matchup, as the Saints’ offense is dangerous. Well, their passing game, anyway. But after an uncharacteristic run-game struggle against the Dolphins, I expect Flores’ group to bounce back against the Vikings’ old nemesis, Alvin Kamara, who also appears banged up, given early injury reports. This comes after newly signed starter Travis Etienne was already placed on IR with a hamstring injury.

The cupboard isn’t bare for the Saints’ offense, though. Head coach Kellen Moore has second-year quarterback Tyler Shough playing well, and the unit currently ranks in the NFL’s top ten in points per game (26.3), net yards (367.0), passing yards (278.5), and first downs (24.3).

That’s fine, but with all due respect to the Lions’, Ravens’, Raiders’, and Falcons’ defenses (especially), the Vikings are playing at heights that even NASA’s most advanced telescope would struggle to reach.

The Saints’ offense revolves around standout wide receiver Chris Olave, and containing him will be the priority. He’s second in the NFL in receiving yards and receptions, has exceeded 100 receiving yards in three of four games, and hasn’t had fewer than eight receptions in any contest. I watched him in Week 1 utterly abuse the Detroit Lions’ secondary, catching 10 passes for 182 yards. The Saints really deserved to win that game.

The Saints’ secret weapon is their dynamic tight end duo of Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant, especially in the red zone. They have six combined receiving touchdowns in just four games. The good news is that, aside from Tucker Kraft and Jonnu Smith in Week 1, the Vikings have held opposing tight ends to just six receptions for 83 yards and no touchdowns in the next three games.

If Flores’ group can match its Week 2 and 3 performance, the Saints will struggle to reach 20 points, home or not.

PREDICTION

For the third straight week, the Vikings will face a desperate team seeking a momentum-shifting win. For the Saints, that means keeping pace with the Atlanta Falcons and the increasingly impressive Carolina Panthers. I picked the Saints to win the NFC South in the preseason, and I truly believe they are better than their 1-3 record suggests. You are what your record says you are, but I think the Saints’ early-January record will better reflect who they really are.

But I don’t believe that turnaround will start this week. They’ll be game, but in the end the Vikings will prove too much on both sides of the ball. Yes, that means the offense finally puts together the complete game the fans have been waiting for. Better late than never. A late Kyler Murray touchdown pass puts this one out of reach.

Minnesota Vikings: 31

New Orleans Saints: 17

item.title: The Bills need more James Cook, but they must stay dedicated to this philosophy
item.description: The Bills have to return to philosophy on offense
item.content:encoded:
Establishing the ideal run-pass variance in an NFL is a challenging balancing act that often looks different for every team. Analytics strongly suggest clubs should be throwing it more than they’re running it, but when you’re a team with an elite back in his prime like the Buffalo Bills there’s always going to be a push from outside observers to more prominently feature the run game.

After Cook only received eight carries through the first three quarters and 12 total in Buffalo’s Week 4 loss to the Patriots, the magnitude of said push intensified.

And sometimes the key to optimizing the ground game stems from when a running play is utilized.

Teams should still be passing on early downs more than they’re running it… particularly when your quarterback is Josh Allen. I wrote about this very philosophy and the logic behind it after Week 1 when the Bills scored 36 points in Houston and did so while throwing on first and second down at the sixth-highest rate among all teams.

After Weeks 1 and 2, the Bills had the eighth-highest early-down passing frequency at 58.0% in non-garbage time scenarios.

In those first two games, Buffalo’s offense was fourth in EPA per play in non-garbage time.

While we can’t be sure the early-down passing caused the outstanding EPA per play for Buffalo’s offense in those opening weeks, the correlation can’t be ignored.

In the next two games that followed, the Bills decided to move away from early-down passing. Their 47.4% pass rate in those scenarios ranked 10th-lowest in Weeks 3 and 4 combined.

Did that track with EPA per play generated by Buffalo’s offense in those contests? Yes it did. The Bills dipped to 16th in EPA per play those two weeks combined.

In the aftermath of the loss to the Patriots, likely all the dedicated pass-game enthusiasts like myself would probably agree Cook needs to get handed the football more than 12 times in a tight game.

HOWEVER, I’m simultaneously advocating for the Bills to take to the air on early downs. In today’s NFL, when margins are as slim as ever, these type of decisions matter.

And staying dedicated to early-down passing has proven to be key to efficiently moving the football.

Sprinkle in Cook when the defense least expects it.

item.title: 3-Point Stance: Josh McDaniels’ diversified offense gets Patriots back on track
item.description: New England’s Week 4 adjustments help the offense find its rhythm.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty-second in pre-snap motion rate and 29th in play-action rate.

Those numbers became a frequent topic of conversation after the New England Patriots’ lopsided 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 3. The figures were cited to explain why the Patriots’ offense ranked near the bottom of the NFL in scoring (31st), averaging just 12 points per game through those first three weeks.

New England’s offense had been stagnant; quarterback Drake Maye struggled to find a rhythm in the pocket, the team fell to 1-2 on the season and its rushing offense ranked dead last in success rate at 28.4%.

But against an undefeated divisional rival, the Buffalo Bills, on Sunday, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels shifted the game plan, and the team exited Orchard Park with a convincing 29-26 victory.

What changed exactly?

Heavy pre-snap motion usage

Leading up to the Week 4 game, McDaniels addressed the offense’s shortcomings by moving players across the formation more frequently.

With New England incorporating pre-snap motion on 75.3% of its offensive snaps — a 21.3% increase from the previous three contests — Buffalo had to adjust on the fly after watching three weeks of film that showcased a largely predictable offense.

By moving their skill players into different formations, the Patriots made it difficult for the Bills to diagnose whether Maye would drop back to pass or hand the ball off to Rhamondre Stevenson or TreVeyon Henderson. McDaniels’ adjustment also seemingly assisted a struggling Maye in grasping a better indication of what Buffalo’s defense was planning, whether a defender followed a moving receiver or shifted their positioning.

While additional factors play into Maye’s improvement and pre-snap motion is not the be-all and end-all indicator, it’s not a coincidence that the signal-caller had his most productive and technically sound performance of the 2026 season when New England ran its most pre-snap motion since Week 15 of 2023.

Maye concluded the matchup passing for 269 yards, three touchdowns and just one interception, leading an eight-play, 73-yard game-winning scoring drive late in the fourth quarter. And even though the third-year quarterback said he’s “always going to be confident” in his ability to make plays after the loss to Jacksonville, it’s evident he was more comfortable operating in the pocket against the Bills.

On the Patriots’ opening drive, Maye and center Jared Wilson fumbled an exchange under center. The third-year quarterback, having to circle the perimeter of the pocket to corral the loose ball, briefly scanned the field three seconds into the play and completed a first-down pass to Hunter Henry. Five plays later, New England took an early 7-0 lead.

McDaniels also increased deception after the snap.

More play-action

The Patriots’ play-action rate increased by 15%, reaching 35.7% of offensive plays on Sunday. New England scored its first touchdown off a play-action snap, using multiple elements to deceive the Buffalo defense.

Maye, receiving a snap from the opposing nine-yard line, faked a screen pass to DeMario Douglas before simulating a handoff to Stevenson. With the Bills blitzing five rushers, Maye fired a pass over the middle of the field, connecting with Romeo Doubs on a skinny post in the end zone.

Play-action adds another layer to the Patriots’ passing game and also benefits the ground attack. Based on New England’s previous usage, running more play-action made the offense harder to diagnose and forced opposing linebackers and defensive backs to respect the pass when the offense lined up in a run look.

And while the offensive line also improved up front at the point of attack, the Patriots’ expanded approach led to a more dynamic offense.

A creative rush attack

Similar to New England’s motion and play-action rates increasing, its run success rate rose to 44.8%. While still below the league average in Week 4, it’s a formidable improvement.

That jump also connects back to McDaniels’ use of pre-snap motion. The tactic appeared more often in the ground game, not just on passing downs.

One advantage of using pre-snap motion before a run play is that it can force a defender to adjust their alignment, potentially pulling bodies away from the run’s intended path. On Sunday, Stevenson rushed for 47 yards and one touchdown on 13 carries, which is a significant improvement from Weeks 1 and 3.

Sunday’s performance offered a blueprint for how the Patriots can expand their offense after three startling weeks to open the season. However, whether McDaniels and Co. maintain these adjustments remains to be seen, starting with New England’s matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders this Sunday.

item.title: Despite play-calling demotion, Davis Webb excited for Broncos’ offense to finally take off
item.description: Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb was disappointed with how the offense performed to start the season but is confident they are close to getting back on track.
item.content:encoded:
The Davis Webb play-calling experiment is officially over. Recently, Head Coach Sean Payton confirmed he would be taking over those duties for Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Chargers.

After four games, the Denver Broncos were in a serious rut on offense. The aerial attack has been erratic, the running game was rarely committed too, and they weren’t putting enough points on the scoreboard. Slow starts have been a common issue throughout the Payton era. However, this year’s early season outing was definitely the worst Broncos Country had witnessed.

Yesterday, Webb spoke offered his thoughts on the situation, reflected on what he had learned, and what he hopes to see from the team moving forward.

“I think it’s more just how we started off offensively,” Webb spoke with where most of his disappointment was centered. Given the team’s talent and additions over the course of the offseason, for the Broncos to be near the bottom of the league in most categories was a significant surprise to many—even with Webb being a first-year play-caller.

“I’m excited to see how our team responds this week. We’ll try to get a team win against a divisional opponent. It was a long week in some ways, but in other ways, it’s back to work,” added Webb.

Truth be told, a lot of it wasn’t on Webb. You can’t really blame him for the team’s penchant for pre-snap penalties. Nor can you assert blame for players failing to execute on the particulars they work hard at on a week-to-week basis. He acknowledged there was a sentiment amongst the offensive players that they had let their offensive coordinator down and acknowledged he will do whatever it takes to help them be successful moving forward.

“No question. I’m very thankful for all those guys, from the offensive line, to the wideouts, the quarterbacks, running backs, tight ends. I’ve definitely felt that, but like I’ve been saying right now, it’s onto the next thing. That’s the NFL. We wake up, and we have a job to do and that’s to help these players be successful. That’s the only thing on my mind right now, and I think our staff’s doing a good job of that.”

As far as Webb’s other responsibilities, everything will stay the same. He will continue to lead the team’s offensive meetings on a weekly basis. Additionally, he will keep close tabs on and be a mentor for Denver’s trio of quarterbacks as the season continues.

Hopefully, this is the weekend the Broncos’ offense finally takes off. The Chargers are banged up on defense and will have several starters out for Sunday’s matchup. Even though they are 0-4, the Broncos can’t afford to underestimate them. Just look at what the Tampa Bay Buccaneers did to the Dallas Cowboys on Thursday Night Football.

Things didn’t turn out the way Webb had hoped. Nevertheless, he remains confident the offense is close to firing on all cylinders moving forward. If so, that should bode well Denver on Sunday and throughout the rest of the regular season.

“Extremely, extremely close. I think there are a few things in the pass game that were close last week, a few things in the run game that were close last week. You can see the second halves of the Jaguars game, the Rams game. I just mentioned three good teams right there. Kansas City was tough on everybody. I think getting off to this start, being at 2-2 is not what we wanted, but it’s where we’re at. I think that a lot of teams in the NFL will be OK with that.”

item.title: What can the Lions defense do vs. Cardinals to earn faith?
item.description: How the Detroit Lions defense can regain some faith this week vs. the Cardinals.
item.content:encoded:
One of the more interesting questions from Dan Campbell’s Friday press conference was about how he can regain confidence in the Detroit Lions defense. In short, what did he need to see in Sunday’s game against the Arizona Cardinals to make him feel better about the direction of the defense.

Campbell’s answer was basically three-fold: force turnovers, get to the quarterback, and cut down significantly on the missed assignment and missed executions.

It’s a fair answer, but probably not one that makes Lions fans feel good enough about the state of the defense. So for today’s Question of the Day, I’m going to ask you the exact same question Campbell was asked:

What would make you feel good about the direction of the defense going into the bye? What benchmarks do you want to see?

My answer: First of all, I want y’all to put your thinking caps on. I know I’m probably going to get at least 50 “Fire Sheppard” answers here, but let’s dig a little deeper.

Before we do, I think it’s at least exploring if there’s anything Detroit can do on Sunday to build faith in the defense. We have to recognize that the Cardinals are not a very good offense right now, and that any “improvement” we see from the Lions could also just be interpreted as facing a poor offense.

That said, I just need to see this team be assignment sound. If Trey McBride and Michael Wilson just win their 1-on-1s, I can live with that as long as Detroit doesn’t have any glaring mental mistakes. If there are terrible run fits, wide open spaces in zones, and failed communications in the secondary, then Detroit can produce as many takeaways as they want—I won’t feel good about this defense making any progress.

If you want to shorten that to one statistical benchmark: no rushes of over 15 yards allowed vs. the Cardinals. The explosive-prone run defense needs to stop or this team has no hope.

Still, I don’t think there’s a ton Detroit can do to make me believe the defense will turn things around based on a single performance against a subpar offense. But they can certainly show progress and lead me to believe they can at least string together some acceptable games of defense.

What specifically—besides firing Kelvin Sheppard—do you want to see this week from the Lions defense?

item.title: Cowboys news: Brian Schottenheimer vows that changes will be made after disappointing loss
item.description: Here is today's Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys had an opportunity to continue their momentum when the 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers came to town on Thursday night. Unfortunately, they were pretty much dominated for four quarters, and head coach Brian Schottenheimer says things will be different going forward as they seek changes.

Team owner Jerry Jones made his disappointment about the game known while the battle was taking place with his reactions as well as afterwards during his postgame interview. On top of the loss, the Cowboys left the matchup with players banged up.

Brian Schottenheimer: Cowboys will ‘absolutely’ make changes, adjustments – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com

The Cowboys were embarrassed by the Buccaneers on Thursday night. As a result, head coach Brian Schottenheimer says the team will shake things up.

“When you are a coach, there are going to be things you’re going to correct,” he said on Friday, in the immediate aftermath of the loss. “We are solution-makers. We’re not excuse-makers, we’re solution-makers. That’s what we’re working on really, really hard right now.

“We’re having the hard conversations. We’re looking at the film. We’re studying the areas [of concern]. Those conversations are really important and we’re having them in all three phases, not just on defense.”

Jerry Jones ‘extraordinarily disappointed’ after Cowboys loss to Buccaneers – Kevin Patra, NFL.com

Cowboys’ owner Jerry Jones was visibly upset watching Dallas get beat by Tampa Bay. After the game, he was detailed as to why he was frustrated.

“Extraordinarily, extraordinarily disappointed,” owner Jerry Jones said of the loss, via the team’s official website. “You really do need to get it done when it’s there to take. They basically were very physical. I thought both their fronts, was really surprised at how well they ran the ball, how they ran it between the tackles. That was surprising.”

The Cowboys left their defeat against the Buccaneers with several key players dealing with injury issues. Their statuses were updated on Friday.

Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said that X-rays on left tackle Tyler Guyton’s back were negative after the team’s 24-16 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday.

Guyton missed the team’s final offensive series and was replaced by former first-round pick Broderick Jones. Guyton was seen holding his back and trying to move around during the timeout before the drive, but the team quickly decided to bring him to the locker room. Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said after the game that Guyton was dealing with a strain. 

5 takeaways from Cowboys’ catastrophe: The most inexcusable Schottenheimer loss – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram

Dallas was bad in all three phases of the game against Tampa Bay. With that said, there wasn’t anything good to say about their performance.

As mentioned above, the cards were laid out for the Cowboys’ defense to get right against Tampa Bay on Thursday. The Buccaneers came into the game allowing the most sacks in the NFL, bottom three in giveaways and had failed to score more than 20 points in three out of four games.

Let’s look at how the defense did with that: one sack, zero takeaways and 24 points allowed. The game plan for Tampa Bay was obvious, to shorten the game with long possessions and quick plays to make life easy for its rookie quarterback. It did exactly that with zero pushback from defensive coordinator Christian Parker’s unit.

Cowboys TE position is a problem that just keeps getting worse – Reid D Hanson, Cowboys Wire

Jake Ferguson had multiple drops against the Buccaneers, with the final one turning into an interception that sealed the game for the Buccaneers. His performance highlighted a huge issue at tight end with the Cowboys.

With 1:22 on the clock, down by eight, and the Cowboys driving deep into Tampa Bay territory, Ferguson took a perfect Dak Prescott pass off the facemask for what would essentially be a game-ending interception. The play counted a staggering -4.4 EPA and marked the biggest shift in win probability of the day, dropping Dallas’ odds down to one percent.

Ferguson’s tragic blunder was the latest of a long list of errors by the 27-year-old veteran. Ferguson has been guilty of dropped passes and costly fumbles for quite some time. His blocking has lacked in both execution and effort and ability to gain yards after the catch have dropped to late-career Jason Witten levels.
